They reached the country which had once been the kingdom of the Scorpion Witch, but found cities there; the woods had become fields; the prince questioned one person and another about the Scorpion Witch and her house, but they answered that their grandfathers had heard from their great, great grandfathers that such silly tales had once been told. “How is that possible!” replied the prince, “I came through this region myself only a short time ago,” and he told them all he knew. The people laughed at him as if he were a lunatic or a person talking in his sleep, and the prince angrily rode on without noticing that his hair and beard were growing white. When he reached the realm of the Woodpecker Fairy, the same questions and answers were exchanged. The prince could not understand how these places had altered so much in a few days, and again rode angrily on. He now had a white beard that reached to his waist, and he felt as if his feet were beginning to tremble. Quitting this country he arrived in his father’s empire. Here he found new people, new towns, and every thing so much changed that he could not recognize it. At last he came to the palace where he was born. When he dismounted, the horse kissed his hand, and said: “I wish you good health, master, I’m going back to the place from which I came. If you want to go too, mount quickly, and we’ll be off.” “Farewell, I too hope to return soon.” The horse darted away with the speed of an arrow. When the prince saw the ruined palace and the weeds growing around it, he sighed deeply and with tears in his eyes tried to remember how magnificent these places had once been. He walked around the building two or three times, tried to recollect how every room, every corner had looked, found the stable where he had discovered the horse, and then went down into the cellar, whose entrance was choked up with fallen rubbish. He groped hither and thither, holding up his eyelids with his hands, and scarcely able to totter along, while his snowy beard now fell to his knees, but found nothing except a dilapidated old chest, which he opened. It seemed empty, but as he raised the lid a voice from the bottom said: “Welcome, if you had kept me waiting much longer, I too should have gone to decay.” Then his death, which had become completely shriveled in the chest, seized him; but the prince fell lifeless on the ground and instantly crumbled into dust.

Into the saddle then I sprung,
The tale to tell to old and young.

title: Punguta Cu Doi Bani
text_english: There was once an old man and an old woman. The old woman had a hen and the old man had a rooster; the old woman's hen laid two eggs a day and she ate a great many, but she would not give the old man a single one. One day the old man lost patience and said: "Listen, old crony, you live as if you were in clover, give me a couple of eggs so that I can at least have a taste of them." "No indeed!" replied the old woman, who was very avaricious. "If you want eggs, beat your rooster that he may lay eggs for you, and then eat them; I flogged my hen, and just see how she lays now." The old man, being stingy and greedy, listened to the old woman's talk, angrily seized his rooster, gave him a sound thrashing and said: "There, now, lay some eggs for me or else go out of the house, I won't feed you for nothing any longer." As soon as the rooster escaped from the old man's hands it ran off down the high-road. While thus pursuing its way, lo and behold! it found a little purse with two half-pennies. Taking it in its beak, the bird turned and went back toward the old man's house. On the road it met a carriage containing a gentleman and several ladies. The gentleman looked at the rooster, saw a purse in its bill, and said to the driver: "Get down and see what this rooster has in its beak." The driver hastily jumped from his box, took the little purse from the rooster's bill, and gave it to his master. The gentleman put it in his pocket and drove on. The rooster was very angry and ran after the carriage, repeating continually: "Kikeriki, sir, Kikerikak, To me the little purse give back." The enraged gentleman said to the coachman as they passed a well: "Take that impudent rooster and throw it into the well." The driver got down from his box again, seized the rooster, and flung it down the well. When the rooster saw that its life was in such great danger, what was it to do? It began to swallow the water, and drank and drank till it had swallowed all the water in the well. Then it flew out and again ran after the carriage, calling: "Kikeriki, sir, Kikerikak, To me the little purse give back." When the gentleman saw this, he was perfectly amazed and said: "Hoho! This rooster is a perfect imp of Satan! Never mind! I'll wring your neck, you saucy cockerel!" When he reached home he told the cook to take the rooster, throw it on the coals burning upon the hearth, and push a big stone in front of the opening in the chimney. The old woman did what her master bade her. When the rooster saw this new injustice, it began to spit out the water it had swallowed till it had poured all the water from the well upon the burning coals. This put out the fire, cooled the hearth, and made such a flood on the kitchen floor that the cook fainted away from pure rage. Then the rooster gave the stone a push, came out safe and sound, ran to the gentleman's window, and began to knock on the panes with its bill, screaming: "Kikeriki, sir, Kikerikak, To me the little purse give back." "Heaven knows that I've got a torment in this monster of a rooster," said the gentleman. "Driver, rid me of it, toss it into the middle of the herds of cows and oxen; perhaps some bull will stick its horns through it and relieve us." The coachman seized the rooster and flung it among the herds. You ought to have seen the rooster's delight. It swallowed bulls, oxen, cows, and calves, till it had devoured the whole herd and its stomach had grown as big as a mountain. Then it went to the window again, spread out its wings before the sun so that it darkened the gentleman's room, and once more began: "Kikeriki, sir, Kikerikak, To me the little purse give back." When the gentleman saw this he was ready to burst with rage and did not know what to do to get rid of the rooster. He stood thinking till at last an idea entered his head: "I'll lock it up in the treasure-chamber. Perhaps if it tries to swallow the ducats one will stick in its throat, and I shall get rid of the bird." No sooner said than done. He grasped the rooster and flung it into the treasure-chamber. The rooster swallowed all the money and left the chests empty. Then it escaped from the room, went to the gentleman's window, and again began: "Kikeriki, sir, Kikerikak, To me the little purse give back." As the gentleman saw that there was nothing else to be done he tossed the purse out. The rooster picked it up, went about its own business, and left the gentleman in peace. All the poultry ran after the rooster so that it really looked like a wedding; but the gentleman turned green with rage as he watched, and said sighing: "Let them all run off to the last chick, I'm glad to be rid of the torment; there was witchcraft in that rooster!" But the puffed-up rooster stalked proudly along, followed by all the fowls, and went merrily on and on till he reached the old man's house and began to crow: "Kikeriki!" When the old man heard the rooster's voice he ran out joyfully to meet the bird, but looking through the door what did he see? His rooster had become a terrible object. An elephant beside it would have seemed like a flea; and following behind came countless flocks of birds, each one more beautiful and brilliant than the other. When the old man saw the rooster so huge and fat, he opened the gate for it. "Master," said the bird,"spread a sheet here in the middle of the yard." The old man, as nimble as a top, laid down the sheet. The rooster took its stand upon it, spread its wings, and instantly the whole yard was filled with birds and herds of cattle, but it shook out on the sheet a pile of ducats that flashed in the sun till they dazzled the eyes. When the old man beheld this vast treasure he did not know what to do in his delight, and hugged and kissed the rooster. But all at once the old woman appeared from somewhere, and when she saw this marvelous spectacle her eyes glittered in her head, and she was ready to burst with wrath. "Dear old friend," she said,"give me a few ducats." "Pine away with longing for them, old woman; when I begged you for some eggs, you know what you answered. Now flog your hen, that it may bring you ducats. I beat my rooster, and you see what it has fetched me." The old woman went to the hen-coop, shook the hen, took it by the tail, and gave it such a drubbing that it was enough to make one weep for pity. When the poor hen escaped from the old woman's hands it fled to the highway. While walking along it found a bead, swallowed it, hurried back home as fast as possible, and began to cackle at the gate. The old woman welcomed it joyfully. The hen ran quickly in at the gate, passed its mistress, and went to its nest—at the end of an hour it jumped off, cackling loudly. The old woman hastened to see what the hen had laid. But when she glanced into the nest what did she perceive? A little glass bead. The hen had laid a glass bead! When the old woman saw that the hen had fooled her, she began to beat it, and beat till she flogged it to death. So the stupid old soul remained as poor as a church-mouse. From that time she might live on roast nothing and golden wait a while, instead of eggs, for she had abused and killed the poor hen, though it was not at all to blame. But the old man was very rich; he built great houses, laid out beautiful gardens, and lived luxuriously. He made the old woman his poultry-maid, the rooster he took about with him everywhere, dressed in a gold collar, yellow boots, and spurs on its heels, so that one might have thought it was one of the Three Kings from the Christmas play instead of a mere ordinary rooster.

title: Soacra Cu Trei Nurori
text_english:
ONCE UPON A TIME THERE WAS AN OLD WOMAN WHO HAD THREE SONS, tall as fir trees and strong in body, but weak in mind. A fairly large landholding, the old family home with all its belongings, a vineyard with a beautiful orchard, livestock and many birds made up the old woman's household. On top of this she had also saved up some coins for rainy days; for she tied every penny with ten knots and trembled over every coin. So as not to scatter her sons away from her side, she had built two more houses nearby, one to the right and one to the left of the old family home. But at the same time she made the firm decision to keep her sons and future daughters-in-law with her — in the old family home — and to arrange nothing regarding the inheritance until close to her death. So she did; and the old woman's heart laughed with joy just thinking how happy she would be, helped by her sons and comforted by her future daughters-in-law. And many times she said to herself: "I will keep watch over my daughters-in-law, I will put them to work, I will keep them in line and I will not let them take a single step out of the house when my sons are away. My mother-in-law — may the earth rest lightly on her! — did the same with me. And my husband — God rest his soul! — could not complain that I deceived him or squandered his household; …although sometimes there were suspicions… and he would scold me… but all that is past now!"

All three of the old woman's sons worked as carters and earned good money. The oldest was reaching the age to marry, and the old woman, sensing this, rushed about to find him a bride; and in five or six villages, she could barely find one to her liking: not too young, tall and lean, but hardworking and obedient. The son did not go against his mother's decision, the wedding was held and the old woman received the mother-in-law's shirt, and one not yet cut at the collar at that, which means the mother-in-law should not be loud-mouthed and constantly grumbling about everything. After the wedding was over, the sons went back to their work, and the daughter-in-law remained with her mother-in-law. That very day, toward evening, the old woman began to lay out the rules of her daughter-in-law's life. For the old woman, a new sieve had no place on the hook. "Why did I make tongs? So I wouldn't burn myself," she used to say. Then she quickly climbed up into the attic and brought down from there a chest of feathers left over from her own deceased mother-in-law, some bundles of hemp and about two measures of millet.

— Here is what I thought you could work on at nights, daughter-in-law. The mortar is in the side room, the spindles are in the basket under the bed, and the distaff is behind the chimney. When you get tired of stripping feathers, you can pound millet; and when your husband comes home from the road, we'll make fish stew with smoked pork ribs from the attic, and Lord, how well we'll eat! For now, to start, while you're still resting, take the distaff at your waist, and by tomorrow morning have these bundles ready for spinning, the feathers stripped and the millet pounded. I'll lie down for a little, for your wedding has worn me to the bone. But you should know that I sleep like a hare; and besides these two eyes, I have another one at the back of my neck, which is always open and with which I see, both night and day, everything that goes on in the house. Did you understand what I told you?

— Yes, mother. Only something to eat…

— Something to eat? An onion, a clove of garlic and a piece of cold cornbread from the shelf is enough for a young wife like you… Milk, cheese, butter and eggs — if only we could scrape some together to take to the market to make a few coins; for the household has gained another mouth to feed and I don't want to lose my standing.

Then, when it grew dark, the old woman lay down in bed facing the wall, so the light from the oil lamp wouldn't bother her, also hinting to her daughter-in-law that she would be watching her; but sleep overtook her immediately, and she had no idea what her daughter-in-law was doing. While the mother-in-law snored away, sleeping soundly, the gentle daughter-in-law bustled about the house; now stripping feathers, now winding thread, now pounding millet and sifting it in a hurry. And if sleep began to weigh on her eyelids, she would immediately take cold water and wash her face, lest the never-sleeping mother-in-law should see her and suspect her. So the poor daughter-in-law toiled until after midnight; but toward dawn, sleep overcame her, and she too fell asleep among the feathers, bundles of hemp, spindles with thread and the sifted millet.

The old woman, who had gone to bed with the chickens, got up before dawn and began slamming and banging about the house, so that the poor daughter-in-law, who had barely dozed off, willingly or not had to get up, kiss her mother-in-law's hand and show her what she had done. Gradually, the daughter-in-law fell into line, and the old woman was satisfied with the choice she had made. A few days later the carters arrived, and the young wife, seeing her dear husband, forgot some of her troubles!

Not much time passed before the old woman arranged things for her middle son too, and found herself a daughter-in-law exactly in the image and likeness of the first one, the only difference being that this one was older and somewhat cross, but fiercely hardworking. After the wedding, the sons went off to their carting again and the daughters-in-law remained at home with their mother-in-law. As was her custom, she gave them measured work and, when evening fell, she went to bed, telling the daughters-in-law to be hardworking and warning them not to fall asleep, for the unsleeping eye would be watching them. The oldest daughter-in-law then explained to the other one about their mother-in-law's all-seeing eye, and so they encouraged each other to work, and the work flowed from their hands. And the mother-in-law lived comfortably.

But good times sometimes await bad ones. Not very long passed before the youngest son also reached marrying age. The old woman however wanted at any cost to have a matching trio of daughters-in-law… and for that reason she had already picked one out in advance. But things don't always go as planned, and sometimes they go quite differently. One fine morning, the son simply brought home a daughter-in-law on his own initiative. The old woman scratched her head, pushed back and forth, but there was nothing to be done, and willingly or not, the wedding was held, and that was that!

After the wedding, the husbands went off again to their work and the daughters-in-law remained at home with their mother-in-law. The old woman again gave them measured work and, when evening came, went to bed as usual. The two older daughters-in-law, seeing the youngest one dawdling at her work, said to her:

— Stop dawdling, for mother can see us.

— How? I can see she's asleep. What kind of nonsense is this? We work and she sleeps?!

— Never mind that she snores, said the middle one, mother has an unsleeping eye at the back of her neck, with which she sees everything we do, and you don't know who mother is yet, you've never tasted her temper.

— At the back of her neck?… she sees everything?… I haven't tasted her temper?… Good thing you reminded me… But what do we eat, girls?

— Just plain patience, dear sister-in-law… And if you're hungry, take a piece of cornbread from the shelf and eat it with some onion.

— Onion with cornbread? Why, no one in my family has ever eaten such food! Isn't there any bacon in the attic? No butter? No eggs?

— There's plenty of everything, said the two, but it all belongs to mother.

— I believe that what belongs to mother belongs to us too, and what is ours belongs to her. Girls! The time for joking is over. You keep working, for I'm going to go prepare something to eat, you know, something more decent; and I'll call you both shortly.

— Lord, what words have come out of your mouth! said the two. Do you want to bring a storm down on our heads? Do you want the old woman to throw us out on the road?

— Don't worry if it gives you a headache! When she asks you, put the blame on me and let me do the talking for everyone.

— Well then… alright!… do as you know how; only don't drag us into trouble too.

— Come on, girls, be quiet, keep your mouths going; for peace doesn't suit me, I love a good quarrel.

And she goes out singing:

Oh, poor foolish man,
What a treasure he was at home!

Not even an hour passed, and a batch of pastries, a few chickens roasted on a spit and fried in butter, a bowl of cheese with cream and a little cornbread were ready. Then she quickly called the other two into the pantry, and they all sat down at the table.

— Come on, girls, eat well and praise the Lord, for I'm rushing to the cellar to bring a small barrel of wine, so these pastries go down better.

After they had eaten and drunk well, they felt like singing, like a Russian at the mouth of the cellar:

Mother-in-law, mother-in-law, sour fruit,
No matter how long you ripen,
Sweet you will never become;
Even if you ripen all autumn,
You're more sour than a cornel berry;
Even if you ripen a year and a summer,
Still sour and bitter you remain;
You come out like a pear gone bad;
You enter the house like a scythe;
You sit in the corner like a stitch in the side.

And they ate, and drank, and sang until they all fell asleep right where they were. When the old woman got up at the crack of dawn, there were no daughters-in-law to be found anywhere. She went outside in a fright, looked this way and that, and when she entered the pantry, what did she see? The poor daughters-in-law were mourning their mother-in-law… Feathers scattered on the floor, crumbs, dishes thrown in all directions, the small barrel of wine overturned — a great mess!

— But what is going on there? cried the old woman in alarm.

The daughters-in-law then jumped up startled; the older ones began to tremble like reeds with fear, and hung their heads in shame. But the one in question answered:

— Why, mother, don't you know that father and mother came, and we made them food, and we brought out a small barrel of wine, and that's why we celebrated a little ourselves. They only just left a little while ago.

— And my in-laws saw me sleeping like that?

— Well how could they not see you, mother?!

— And why didn't you wake me? May plague consume you!

— Well, mother, these girls said that you see everything; and so I thought you were angry with father and mother and that's why you didn't get up. And they were so saddened that the food barely agreed with them.

— Well, you wretches, I'll give you a proper beating from now on!

And from then on the daughters-in-law no longer had a good day in the house with the old woman. Whenever she remembered those plump, fat little chickens, the wine from the cellar, the waste that was made of her hard work, and that her in-laws had seen her sleeping there sprawled out like that, she would burst with anger and gnaw at the daughters-in-law the way a woodworm gnaws at timber. Even the two older ones had grown thoroughly sick of the old woman's sharp tongue; and the youngest now found the opportunity to settle the score with her and at the same time arrange the old woman's inheritance through an unprecedented will, and here is how:

— Sisters-in-law, she said one day, when they were alone in the vineyard. We cannot live in this house unless we do everything possible to rid ourselves of this old hag.

— Well, how?

— Do as I teach you, and don't worry about a thing.

— What should we do? asked the oldest.

— Look, we'll burst into the old woman's house, and you grab her by the scruff of the neck and slam her head against the east wall as hard as you can; and you do the same with her head against the west wall, and then you'll see what else I'll do to her.

— But what about when our husbands come home?

— Then you two play dead silent, don't say a word. I'll handle them too, and don't worry if anything comes of it!…

The other two were persuaded, they all entered the house; grabbed the old woman by the hair and slammed her head against the walls until they dazed her. Then the youngest, being more mischievous than the other two, throws the old woman in the middle of the room and kneads her with her feet, and thrashes her thoroughly; then she pulls out her tongue, pierces it with a needle and sprinkles it with salt and pepper, so that the tongue immediately swelled up, and the poor mother-in-law could no longer say a single word; but she had not entirely lost her senses. Then the daughters-in-law, following the advice of the one in question, laid the old woman in clean bedding, to remind her of when she was a bride; and after this they began pulling rolls of linen from the old woman's chest, nudging each other and talking about shrouds, walking sticks, biers, bridges, the coin placed in the dead person's hand, about the chickens or sheep to be given over the grave, about ghosts and all manner of other terrifying superstitions — which alone were more than enough to put the poor old woman into her grave. So this is how the happiness she had dreamed of before came to pass!

While all this was happening, some carts were heard creaking: the husbands were coming. Their wives went out to meet them and, following the youngest one's advice, from the gate they threw themselves around their husbands' necks and began talking to them and flattering each one more sweetly than the last.

— But how is mother? they all asked at once while unyoking the oxen.

— Mother, the youngest cut in before the others could speak, mother is not doing well; it seems she intends to leave us, poor soul.

— What? said the husbands, alarmed, dropping the yoke pins from their hands.

— What? Look, it's been about five or six days since she went to take the calves to pasture, and a bad wind must have come over her, poor soul!… The fairies took her mouth and her legs.

The sons then all rushed into the house to their mother's bedside; but the poor old woman was swollen like a barrel and couldn't even blink her mouth; however she had not entirely lost her awareness. And seeing them, she moved her hand slightly and pointed to the oldest daughter-in-law and the east wall, then pointed to the middle one and the west wall; then to the youngest and down to the middle of the room; after that she could barely bring her hand toward her mouth and immediately fell into a terrible faint. Everyone was crying and could not make sense of the signs their mother was making. Then the young daughter-in-law said, pretending to cry herself:

— Don't you understand what mother wants?

— No, they said.

— Poor mother is leaving her last wishes: that the oldest brother should take the land and the house to the east; the middle one, the one to the west; and we, as the youngest, should remain here, in the old family home.

— How right you are, wife, answered her husband.

Then the others, having nowhere left to hesitate, the will was considered properly made. The old woman died that very day, and the daughters-in-law, with hair unbound, wailed over her so that the village rang with it. Then, two days later, they buried her with great honor, and all the women from the village and from the neighboring areas talked about the mother-in-law with three daughters-in-law and said: "Lucky is she that she died, for surely there are those to mourn her”

title: Capra Cu Trei Iezi
text_english: ONCE UPON A TIME THERE WAS A GOAT WHO HAD THREE KIDS. The oldest and the middle one were mischievous troublemakers; while the little one was hardworking and wise. As the saying goes: "There are five fingers on one hand and they don't all resemble one another." One day, the goat calls the kids in from outside and says to them: — My dear little children! I am going into the forest to bring back some food. But you, lock the door after me, listen to one another, and don't you dare open it until you hear my voice. When I come back, I will let you know, so that you recognize me, and I will say to you like this: Three little horned kids, Unlock your mother's door! For mother brings you: Leaves in her mouth, Milk in her udders, A lump of salt On her back, A little cornbread On her heel, A bunch of flowers Under her arms. Did you hear what I said? — Yes, little mother, said the kids. — Can I trust you? — Don't worry at all, little mother, the older ones rushed to say first. We are men of our word, and what we've said once stays said. — If that's so, then come and let mother kiss you! May God protect you from all evil, and farewell for now! — Go safely, little mother, said the little one, with tears in his eyes, and may God help you to return safely and bring us food. Then the goat leaves and goes about her business. And the kids close the door after her and slide the bolt. But as the old saying goes: "Walls have ears and windows have eyes." An enemy wolf — and you know which one? — The very godfather of the goat, who had long been waiting for the right moment to devour the kids, was eavesdropping at the wall behind the house while the goat was talking with them. "Good!" he said to himself. "Now is my time… If sin pushes them to open the door for me, good luck to me! I know I'd flesh them out and pluck them clean!" No sooner said than done, he comes to the door; and as he comes, he begins: Three little horned kids, Unlock your mother's door! For mother brings you: Leaves in her mouth, Milk in her udders, A lump of salt On her back, A little cornbread On her heel, A bunch of flowers Under her arms. — Come! Open quickly, my dear ones, quickly! — Hey! Boys, said the oldest, jump up and open the door, mother is coming with food. — Poor me! said the little one. Don't you dare do the foolish thing of opening it, or woe will be upon us! That is not our mother. I recognize her by her voice; her voice is not so thick and hoarse, but thinner and more beautiful! The wolf, hearing this, went to a blacksmith and had his tongue and teeth sharpened to make his voice thinner, and then, returning, he began again: Three little horned kids, Unlock your mother's door!… — Well, you see, said the oldest again; do I always have to agree with you? It IS mother, it IS mother! And who else would it be if not her?! I have ears too! I'm going to open it for her. — Brother! Brother! said the little one again. Listen to me too! Maybe later someone will come and say: Open the door, Your auntie has come! and then would you absolutely have to open it? Don't you know that auntie has been dead since the white wolves roamed and she's turned to dust, poor soul? — Well then! Wasn't I right? said the oldest. Look, things went bad in the world from the moment the tail started being the head… If you listen to him, you'll keep mother outside for a long time. I, for one, am going to open the door. Then the youngest quickly hid himself in the chimney and, bracing his feet on the ledge and his nose covered in soot, he goes silent as a fish and trembles like a reed with fear. But fear comes from heaven, poor thing! Likewise the middle one, whoosh! quickly under a chest; he curls up there as best he can, silent as the earth, his flesh trembling with fear. Running away is shameful, but it keeps you healthy!… But the oldest goes behind the door and — should he pull, shouldn't he pull? — in the end, he pulls the bolt… And then!… what does he see? And does he even have time to see?… because the wolf's eyes were blazing and his throat was hissing with hunger. And, without a second thought, snap! he grabs the kid by the neck, slices off his head on the spot and eats him so quickly and with such appetite, it seemed as if he hadn't even had a bite to put on a single tooth. Then he licks his muzzle neatly and begins to pace restlessly around the house, saying: — I don't know, did my imagination deceive me, or did I hear more voices? But what on earth?! It's as if they sank into the ground… Where could they be, where could they be? He peeks here, peeks there, but nothing! The kids are nowhere! — My!… what a great mystery this is!… but I have no scythe at home either… let me rest these old bones a little! Then he bends his back with some difficulty, and sits down on the chest. And when he sat on the chest, I don't know how it happened, but either the chest cracked, or the godfather sneezed… Then the kid under the chest, could he stay silent? — sin was eating at him and his back was itching, poor little thing! — Bless you, godfather! — Ah!… you little rascal! Here you were? Come over here to your dear godfather, let him give you a kiss! Then he lifts the chest gently, grabs the kid by the ears and tosses him about and plucks him clean too — feathers flying!… As the saying goes: "Every bird perishes by its own tongue." Afterward he wanders around the house a while longer, hoping to find something more, but finds nothing, for the wise little kid was keeping perfectly quiet in the chimney, as silent as a fish in broth on the fire. When the wolf sees and sees that he can find nothing more, he sets his mind to one thing: he arranges the two heads with their teeth grinning in the windows, so that it seemed they were smiling; then he smears all the walls with blood, to spite the goat even more, and then leaves and goes on his way. As soon as the enemy left the house, the little kid quickly climbs down from the chimney and locks the door well. Then he begins scratching his head and weeping bitterly for his little brothers. — My dear little brothers! If only they hadn't given in, the wolf wouldn't have eaten them! And poor mother doesn't know of this great calamity that has fallen upon her! And he cries and cries until he nearly faints! But what could he do? The fault was not his, and they got what they went looking for. While he was mourning like this, there came the goat, hurrying as fast as she could, loaded with food and panting. And as she came, from far away she sees the two heads, with grinning teeth, in the windows. — My dear little darlings, dear! How they wait with joy and smile at me when they see me! Mother's boys, oh boys, Beautiful and little-horned! The goat's joy was no small thing. But when she came closer — what did she see? A chill cold as ice passes through her veins, her legs give way, a trembling seizes her whole body, and her eyes go blurry. And what was there was not a good thing!… She still walks to the door as best she can, thinking that her imagination was deceiving her… and when she arrives, she begins: Three little horned kids, Unlock your mother's door! For mother brings you: Leaves in her mouth, Milk in her udders, A lump of salt On her back, A little cornbread On her heel, A bunch of flowers Under her arms. Then the youngest kid — who was now both the first and the last — jumps up quickly and opens the door for her. Then he throws himself into his mother's arms and with tears of blood begins to tell her: — Mother, mother, look at what happened to us! Great fire and flood have fallen upon our heads! The goat then, staring wide-eyed around the house, is seized with terror and stands frozen!… But then, gathering her courage, she came a little to her senses and asked: — But what happened here, child? — What could have happened, mother? Look, as soon as you left home, not much time had passed and someone was heard knocking at the door and saying: Three little horned kids, Unlock your mother's door… — And?… — And my oldest brother, foolish and restless as you know him, ran to the door to open it. — And then?… — Then I quickly hid in the chimney, and my middle brother in the chest, while the oldest, as I told you, carelessly goes behind the door and pulls the bolt!… — And then?… — Then, great horror! Our godfather and your friend, the godfather wolf, appears right there in the doorway! — Who? My godfather? Him? The one who swore on his own fur that he would never frighten my little children? — Well yes, mother! As you can see, he frightened them completely! — Well, I'll teach him a lesson! Because he sees I'm a poor widow with a house full of children, he thinks he can mock my home? And put you into storage? No deed goes unpunished… The wretched, shameless creature! He even used to grin at me sometimes and wink with his tooth… But I'm not the kind he thinks I am: I have never jumped over fences my whole life. Well, just you wait, godfather, I'll give you a proper beating! You thought you could cross me? Just remember — you'll come out of it without horns! — Oh, mother, oh! Better be quiet and leave him to God's will! You know there's a saying: "Don't see the devil, but don't cross yourself either!" — No, my dear! "Until you reach God, the saints take your soul." And remember what I tell you, child: if he ever dares to sniff around here again, just wait!… Only you, don't breathe a word to anyone, so he doesn't get wind of it. And from then on she too watched and waited for the right moment to settle the score with her godfather. She puts herself to thinking and weighs things up, how to fix it and what to do to him? "Aha! Now I've found the remedy for him," she said to herself. "Quiet! I'll do one thing to my godfather that will make him bite his own paws!" Near her house there was a deep pit; that was the goat's hope. — To the tub with fire, godfather wolf, there's no other way!… Now the deed begins: To work, godmother, for the wolf has given you plenty to do! And so saying, she tucks up her skirts, rolls up her sleeves, stokes the fire and sets about making food. She makes stuffed cabbage rolls, she makes fish stew, she makes cornmeal cakes, she makes cheesecake with cream and eggs and all kinds of dishes. Then she fills the pit with embers and rotten wood, so the fire burns smoldering. After that she places a wicker grate only loosely supported and some leafy branches over it; over the branches she pours soil and over the soil she spreads a mat. Then she makes a small stool of wax especially for the wolf. Afterward she leaves the food on the fire to boil and goes through the forest to find her godfather and invite him to the feast. She walks and walks through the woods, until she comes across a terrible dark ravine and on a quiet path she runs straight into the wolf. — Good day, godmother! What wind has blown you this way? — May your heart be as good as your looks, godfather… well, you know yourself that need takes you where you don't want to go. Look, I don't know who was at my home in my absence, but I know they did me a fine trick! — How so, dear godmother? — Look, they found the kids alone, killed them and tore them apart, I wept for them out of pity! Only a widow should never be left alone! — You don't say, godmother! — Well now, whether I say it or don't, it's all the same to me. Well, the little ones have gone to the Lord, and duty calls us to care for their souls. That is why I made a memorial feast, as best I could, and I thought it fitting to invite you too, godfather; to comfort me… — Gladly, dear godmother, but I'd have been even more glad if you had invited me to a wedding. — I believe you, godfather, but well, things don't go as we wish, but as the One Above wills. Then the goat sets off ahead weeping, and the wolf follows her, pretending to weep. — Lord, godfather, Lord! she said sighing. The very thing you love most in the world — that's what you lose… — Well yes, godmother, if a person knew what would happen to them, they would protect themselves in advance. Don't take it so hard, for one day we will all go there. — That's true, godfather, no doubt. But the poor little ones, how young they were when they left! — Well yes, godmother; it seems God also likes the younger tender ones. — Well, if God had taken them, what would you do? But like this?… — Lord, godmother, Lord! I'll do as the simpleton does… Could it be that uncle Martin paid you a visit at home? For I remember as if it were now that I once met him in the raspberry bushes; and he told me that if you would give him one of the boys, he would teach him the furrier's trade. And from word to word, from one thing to another, they arrive at the godmother's home! — Come in, godfather, she said, taking the little stool and placing it on top of the pit in question, sit there and eat a little of what God has given us! She then overturns the stuffed cabbage rolls into a bowl and sets them before him. Then our wolf begins to eat greedily; and gulp, gulp, gulp, the cabbage rolls were going down his throat whole. — God rest the departed, godmother, for you have made such good cabbage rolls! And as he was feasting, thud! he falls senseless into the pit of embers, for the wax stool had melted, and the grate over the pit was not well supported: neither better nor worse, as if made for the godfather. — Well, well! Now pull out, wolf, what you have eaten! You thought you could cross the goat? The goat has gotten the better of you! — Mercy, godmother, my feet! Please pull me out, my heart is burning inside me! — No, godfather; because that's how my heart burned too, for my little kids! God likes the younger tender ones; but I also like the older ones, as long as they are well roasted; you know, so the fire has passed right through them. — Godmother, I am scorching, I am burning completely, I am dying, don't leave me! — Burn, godfather, die, for you are no good alive either! It will barely pass for that poor child, the fright he had, since I would have needed a lot of fur from you to smoke him with. Do you remember, wicked and foul beast, when you swore on your own fur? And how nicely you ate my little kids! — My heart is stinging inside me, godmother! Please pull me out, and don't burden yourself so much with my sin! — Death for death, godfather, burn for burn, for you spoke nicely earlier with words from scripture! After this, the goat and the kid took a pile of hay and threw it over him, into the pit, to calm the fire a little. Then, in the end, they fell upon him and struck him on the head with rocks and whatever they could grab, until they killed him completely. And so the poor goat lost her two kids, but she also settled accounts with her godfather wolf, and settled she remained. And hearing the neighboring goats of such a thing, they were very pleased! And they all gathered for the wake and set themselves to eating and drinking, celebrating together… And I was there myself, and right after that I quickly mounted a saddle, and came and told you the story just like that, and then I mounted a wheel and told you the whole tale; and then I mounted a strawberry and told you, good people, one great big whopping lie!

title: Salt in Food
text_english: Once upon a time, as it always begins. There was once an emperor. This emperor had three daughters. Having been left a widower, he had poured all his love upon his daughters. They, having grown up and seeing the care their father put into raising them, educating them and protecting them from all harm and trouble, also strove with all their strength to make him forget the grief that had come over him at the death of their mother. One day, it came to the emperor to ask his oldest daughter: — My daughter, how do you love me? — How do I love you, father? — I love you like honey, she answered, after thinking about what could be the sweetest thing in the world. That was as far as her mind took her, and that was what she said. — God bless you, my daughter; may God grant me the joy of having you. And asking his middle daughter too: — And you, how do you love me, my daughter? — Like sugar, father. That was as far as her mind took her too, and that was what she answered. — May God give you well, my daughter. May you bring me joy. It seems these daughters were flatterers and knew how to show more love toward their father than they actually felt. The emperor rejoiced greatly when he heard from his older daughters how much they loved him. He thought that no other kind of love could exist than one sweet as honey and sugar. And looking at his youngest daughter, who stood a little apart and shyly, he asked her too: — How do you love me, my daughter? — Like salt in food, father! she answered with a serene face, smiling with natural affection and lowering her eyes in shyness at having spoken. She was embarrassed, poor thing, seeing that her father had noticed her too, being the youngest that she was. When her sisters heard the answer she gave their father, they burst out laughing and turned their faces away from her. And their father frowned and, full of anger, said: — Come here, you foolish girl, let us have a word. Did you not hear your older sisters, with what kind of love they love me? How did you not follow their example and tell me how much sweet love you also have for your father? Is this what I get for struggling to raise you and give you an education like no others in the world? Be gone from me, you and your salt with you! When the emperor's youngest daughter heard the wrath of her father falling upon her head, she sank into the depths of the earth with grief that her father was angry, and gathering her courage, said: — Forgive me, father, I did not mean to upset you. I reasoned in my own mind that the love I have for you is, if not greater than that of my sisters, then no less than honey and sugar either... — Listen, listen, her father interrupted her; and you still have the nerve to compare yourself to your older sisters? Be gone from me, shameless girl that you are, don't let me hear your name again! He shut her up and left her crying. Her sisters wanted to comfort her, but with words that stung and did her more harm than good. The emperor's youngest daughter, seeing that even her sisters did not spare her, put her hope in God and decided to leave wherever the Lord's mercy would take her. She therefore took from her father's house a set of poor, old clothes and wandered from village to village, until she reached the court of another emperor. Arriving there, she stood at the gate. The head housekeeper saw her and when she came to her asked what she wanted; she answered that she was a poor girl without parents and would like to enter service if there was a place. Just then the housekeeper's assistant had left and she wished to take on another. The housekeeper looked at her with sharp eyes and thought she seemed good enough to take into service. The emperor's daughter was also asked what wage she wanted, and she answered that she wanted no wage at all, only to serve for a while and if her service proved worthy of any wage, to be given as much as it was worth. The housekeeper was pleased seeing her answer so wisely, and took her on as her assistant. She told her what she had to do and put in her hands a large bunch of keys from among the many she had. The girl was wise and clever. She began to tidy the pantry and the cupboards for which she had the keys and to put every little thing in its proper order. And since she had a skilled hand at kneading, making preserves and other food delicacies found in the pantries of emperors, the provisions of the court were left in her care. And how could she not have known how to do all these things? Was she not, after all, an emperor's daughter? And not a single complaint arose from anyone, for she divided all the provisions with balance and fairness, and no one could find any favoritism in her. Never would she stand around in idle talk, or with the strangers who came to collect their provisions and rations. Never would an unguarded word escape her lips, nor would she listen to such words from anyone, for she would feel ashamed and found words proper enough to silence even the most loose-tongued. She did not gossip with the servants or maids of the court, but when she found a little time to rest, she read from a book. Everyone held her in great respect and no one could find any fault in her to hang against her. News of the worthiness and humility of the head housekeeper's assistant soon reached the ears of the empress herself. She wished to see her. And when the emperor's daughter presented herself to the empress, she knew how to present herself and speak with a pure heart, without pretense and without too much boldness. The empress began to grow fond of her. She suspected that the housekeeper's assistant could not be of low birth. And so, as I told you, the empress took the girl, the housekeeper's assistant, to be near her. Wherever the empress went, she went too; when the empress sat down to work, she worked too. And the work that came from her hands was like pearls, nothing less. From all the wise words that came from her mouth, the empress liked her more than anything. Why say more? She had come to be inseparable from the empress. The empress loved her like her own child. Even the emperor marveled at such attachment of the empress to this girl. This emperor had only one son. His father and mother looked upon him like the sun. They doted on him. And when the emperor went to war, he took his son with him, so that he might learn the ways of warfare. There, somehow, in some way, he was brought home wounded. You should have seen his mother's grief and weeping. She turned her nights into days watching over him in his illness. And when exhaustion overtook her so that she could no longer stand on her feet, the empress put her household girl, as a trusted person, to care for him, and then, one or the other of them, was never absent from the wounded one's bedside. The girl's gentle and wise words, her sweet and genuine comforts, her humility awakened in the sick young man a feeling he had never had before, and more than anything, the way she knew how to move so gently when she changed his bandages, made the emperor's son love her like a sister, for it seemed she eased his pain whenever she laid her hand on his wounds. One afternoon, after he had gotten better, while talking with his mother, he said to her: — You know what, mother, I have a mind to get married. — Good, my dear, good. Better while young than to be swept up in the waves of life. Let your mother find you a good girl, of imperial blood and worthy character. — She is already found, mother. — And who is she? Do I know her? — Don't be upset, mother, if I tell you. My heart has remained with your household girl. I love her, mother, like my own soul. Of all the imperial and noble daughters I have seen, none has pleased me like her. She has captured my heart. The empress resisted somewhat, she pushed back; but it was not possible to turn her son's inclination away from this marriage. When she saw and saw that it could not be otherwise, and that the girl her son had chosen to take as wife was wise, gentle, of good judgment, and above all humble, honest and worthy, she agreed too. It remained now to also persuade the emperor, the boy's father, to accept their son's choice as well. This was not a great difficulty; for both the mother and the son fell to pleading and praised the girl as well as they knew how. So the emperor and empress betrothed their son to the empress's household girl and set the date for the wedding. When they began making the wedding invitations, the emperor's son's betrothed prayed with all her heart that the emperor such-and-such, meaning her father, should also be invited to the wedding. She was careful, however, not to tell anyone that she was that emperor's daughter. Her in-laws agreed to grant her wish and invited that emperor to the wedding as well. On the day of the wedding all the guests came. The celebrations began and lasted all day, as befits emperors — what can you say? In the evening a grand imperial table was laid out, with all manner of food, drinks, pastries and other delicacies that would make you lick your fingers eating them. The bride had ordered the cooks what dishes to prepare. But she herself, with her own hands, prepared separately all those same dishes only for one guest. She then gave orders to a trusted servant to pay careful attention that when bringing to the table the dishes she had prepared, they should be placed before the invited emperor who had come at her request. But to be careful not to place them before anyone else, for there would be mortal danger. The trusted servant did exactly as he was ordered. After all the guests sat at the table, they began to eat and make merry beyond description. The invited emperor, meaning the bride's father, ate but not really. Even from the moment he had arrived, he kept looking at the bride and it seemed his heart was telling him something, but he couldn't bring himself to believe his own eyes. It seems he was recognizing his child, and being unable to understand how she had come to marry an emperor's son, he did not dare say anything to anyone. You see, the hardships and troubles the poor girl had suffered had changed her from how her father had known her. And being stirred by the appetite with which the other guests were eating, he would have liked to eat and make merry too; but after he tasted once or twice from his dishes, he stopped. The servant who brought him dishes was taking them away whole and untouched. This emperor was puzzled as to how all the other guests were eating with such appetite dishes that had no taste for him at all. He ventured to ask his neighbor on the right. This one answered that he hadn't eaten such good food in as long as he could remember. The emperor tasted from his neighbor's plate and saw that the food was indeed good. He did the same with his neighbor on the left. His mouth watered for the good food he had tasted from his neighbors; hunger urged him to eat too; but who could eat the dishes that were being brought to him? He endured as best he could; out of shame he would sometimes take a little from the dishes brought to him, so as not to embarrass himself among the guests, but otherwise nothing. In the end he could hold back no longer, and standing up, he said in a loud voice: — Really, emperor, did you invite me to your son's wedding to mock me? — Goodness, your majesty! How could such a thought enter your mind? As the whole gathering can see, I honor you as I honor all the other emperors, without distinction. — Forgive me, emperor, but all the other guests' dishes are good to eat, only mine are not. The father-in-law emperor was furious and ordered that the cooks should come immediately to account for what they had done, and the guilty ones to be put to death. Do you know what the matter was? The bride had prepared all the dishes for her father without salt, but only with honey and sugar. Even the salt cellar in front of him was filled with ground sugar, and in vain did the poor emperor take from the salt cellar with his knife what he believed to be salt and put it in his food — the food, instead of becoming better, became even sweeter than it already was, and even more unpalatable. Then the bride stood up and said to the father-in-law emperor: — I prepared the dishes for the emperor who is upset, and here is why I did it: This emperor is my father. We were three sisters in our father's house. Father asked us one day how we loved him. My older sisters, one answered that she loved him like honey, the other like sugar. I told him that I loved him like salt in food. That is how I reasoned that there could be no greater love than this! Father was angry with me and drove me from home. God did not let me perish and, through hard work, honesty and diligence, I reached where you see me now. I wanted to prove to my father that without honey and without sugar a person can live, but without salt they cannot — that is why I prepared his dishes without salt. Judge for yourselves with your imperial wisdom who was right. All the guests in one voice found it fitting that the girl had been wrongly driven from her father's house. Then the girl's father confessed that he had not known how to appreciate the spirit of his daughter and asked for forgiveness. The girl too kissed his hand and asked for forgiveness herself if her deed had upset him. And they set themselves to such merrymaking and celebration that word of it spread throughout the world. The girl's father made merry, or maybe not quite, but the father-in-law certainly made merry and took pride in having gained such a daughter-in-law, of good lineage, wise and hardworking. I too was at the wedding together with that bald fellow who is hiding among you, honored lords. Many bones, my lord, fell from that table, and whichever fell, they all landed on the bald man's head. And I mounted a saddle and told it to you just like that. And I mounted a short spoon — long live those who listened. And I also mounted a spindle — long live those who told it.

title: The old man's daughter and the old woman's daughter
text_english: ONCE UPON A TIME THERE WAS AN OLD MAN AND AN OLD WOMAN; and the old man had a daughter, and the old woman also had a daughter. The old woman's daughter was ugly, lazy, vain and mean-hearted; but because she was her mother's daughter, she was pampered like a crow in a snare, leaving all the hard work to the old man's daughter. The old man's daughter, however, was beautiful, hardworking, obedient and good-hearted. God had adorned her with all the good and beautiful gifts. But this good girl was tormented both by her stepsister and her stepmother; luckily God had made her a hardworking and patient girl; for otherwise things would have gone very badly for her. The old man's daughter up the hill, the old man's daughter down the valley; she after firewood through the forest, she with the sack on her back to the mill, she, in the end, everywhere after work. As long as the day lasted, she never rested her feet; she came from one direction and went off in another. And the old woman and her precious daughter were still grumbling and dissatisfied. For the old woman, the old man's daughter was a millstone around the house; while her own daughter was basil fit to be placed by the icons. When both girls went to the village spinning gatherings in the evening, the old man's daughter never wasted time, but spun a sieve full of spindles; while the old woman's daughter with great effort spun just one spindle; and then, when both girls came home late at night, the old woman's daughter quickly jumped over the fence and told the old man's daughter to hand her the sieve with the spindles, to hold it while she jumped over too. Then the old woman's daughter, cunning as she was, took the sieve and ran into the house to the old woman and the old man, saying that she had spun those spindles. In vain did the old man's daughter say afterward that this was the work of her own hands; for immediately the old woman and her daughter would attack her and it had to remain theirs. When Sundays and holidays came, the old woman's daughter was dolled up and groomed, as if the calves had licked her. There was no dance, no communal work gathering in the village to which the old woman's daughter did not go, while the old man's daughter was strictly kept away from all of these. And then, when the old man came home from wherever he had been, the old woman's mouth ran like a hemp-brake; that his daughter didn't listen, that she was idle, that she was lazy, that she was bad stock... this and that; and that she should be driven from the house; that she should be sent to service wherever she liked, for it was impossible to keep her any longer; because she might corrupt her own daughter too. The old man, being a simpleton, or however you wish to call him, looked to her for everything, and whatever she said was sacred. In his heart, poor old man, he might have said something more; but now the hen had started crowing in his house and the rooster had no more standing; and besides, God forbid he should dare to argue with that shrew; for the old woman and her daughter would fill him with a barrage of abuse. One day, the old man, very bitter from all the old woman had told him, called his daughter and said to her: — My dear, look what your mother keeps telling me about you: that you don't obey her, that you are sharp-tongued and corrupted and that it is impossible for you to stay in my house any longer; for this reason, go wherever God will guide you, so that there may be no more quarreling in this house on your account. But I advise you, as a father, that wherever you go, be obedient, gentle and hardworking; for in my house you got along as you got along — because there was also a father's mercy at hand!... but among strangers, God knows what sort of people you will come across; and they will not be able to bear from you what we have borne. Then the poor girl, seeing that the old woman and her daughter wanted by any means to drive her away, kissed her father's hand and, with tears in her eyes, set off into the wide world, moving away from her parental home with no hope of return! And she walked and walked along a road, until by chance a little dog came before her, sick as could be and so thin you could count her ribs; and when she saw the girl, she said to her: — Beautiful and hardworking girl, have pity on me and care for me, for I will be useful to you one day! Then the girl felt compassion and, taking the little dog, washed her and cared for her very well. Then she left her there and continued on her way, satisfied in her soul that she had been able to do a good deed. She had not walked very far when she saw a beautiful pear tree in bloom, but covered all over with caterpillars. The pear tree, seeing the girl, said: — Beautiful and hardworking girl, care for me and clean me of caterpillars, for I will be useful to you one day! The girl, hardworking as she was, cleaned the pear tree of dead growth and caterpillars with great care and then continued on her way to find a master. And walking further, she suddenly saw a muddy and neglected well. The well then said: — Beautiful and hardworking girl, care for me, for I will be useful to you one day! The girl cleaned the well and cared for it very well; then left it and continued on her way. And walking further still, she suddenly came upon an oven that was crumbling and nearly falling apart. The oven, seeing the girl, said: — Beautiful and hardworking girl, plaster me and care for me, for I may be useful to you one day! The girl, who knew that working never caused anyone's tail to fall off, rolled up her sleeves, trod the clay and plastered the oven, whitewashed it and cared for it until it was a pleasure to look at! Then she washed her hands nicely of the clay and set off again on the road. And walking now both day and night, she somehow lost her way; yet she did not lose her hope in God, but walked straight ahead until one day, early in the morning, passing through a dark forest, she came upon a very beautiful clearing, and in the clearing she saw a little house shaded by some weeping willows; and when she approached that house, an old woman came out to meet the girl gently and said to her: — But what are you looking for in these parts, child, and who are you? — Who should I be, auntie? Look, a poor girl, without mother or father, I can say; only the One Above knows how much I have suffered since the mother who bore me folded her hands on her chest! I am looking for a master and, knowing no one and wandering from place to place, I have lost my way. But God has guided me to your house and I beg you to give me shelter. — Poor girl! said the old woman. Truly only God has guided you to me and saved you from danger. I am Holy Sunday. Serve me today and be assured that tomorrow you will not leave my house empty-handed. — Very well, little mother, but I don't know what chores I must do. — Just wash my little children, who are sleeping now, and feed them; then make me some food; and when I return from church, let me find it neither cold nor hot, but just right to eat. And as she said it, the old woman set off to church, while the girl rolled up her sleeves and set to work. First of all she prepared the bathing water, then went outside and began to call: — Children, children, children! Come to mother to be washed! And when the girl looked, what did she see? The yard had filled and the forest was swarming with a multitude of dragons and all sorts of creatures large and small! But strong in faith and with her hope in God, the girl was not frightened; instead she took them one by one and washed them and cared for them as well as could be. Then she set about making the food, and when Holy Sunday came from church and saw the children washed beautifully and all the chores done well, she was filled with joy; and after she sat at the table, she told the girl to go up into the attic and choose from there whatever chest she wished and to take it as her wages; but not to open it until she was home, at her father's. The girl went up into the attic and saw there a multitude of chests: some older and uglier, others newer and more beautiful. But she, not being greedy, chose the oldest and ugliest of them all. And when she came down with it, Holy Sunday frowned slightly, but could do nothing. She blessed the girl, who took the chest on her back and returned toward her parental home with joy, along the same road she had come. On the road, there was the oven she had plastered, full of pastries, risen and golden-brown... And the girl ate pastries, and ate, splendidly; then took a few more for the road and set off. Further along, there was the well she had cared for, full to the brim with water clear as a tear, sweet and cold as ice. And on the well's edge were two silver cups, from which she drank water until she was refreshed. Then she took the cups with her and continued forward. And walking further, there was the pear tree she had cared for, loaded with pears, yellow as wax from ripeness, and sweet as honey. The pear tree, seeing the girl, bent its branches downward; and she ate pears and took along the road as many as she needed. From there, walking further, she met the little dog again, who was now strong and beautiful, and around her neck she wore a necklace of gold coins which she gave to the girl, as thanks for having cared for her in her illness. And from here, the girl, continuing forward, arrived home at her father's. The old man, when he saw her, his eyes filled with tears and his heart with joy. The girl then took out the necklace and the silver cups and gave them to her father; then opening the chest together, countless herds of horses, droves of cattle and flocks of sheep came out of it, so that the old man instantly felt younger, seeing such riches! But the old woman was left seething and did not know what to do with herself from spite. The old woman's daughter then took her courage in her teeth and said: — Don't worry, mother, the world is not robbed of riches; I'll go and bring you even more. And as she said it, she set off with spite, fuming and raging. She walked as much as she walked, along the same road where the old man's daughter had been; she too met the thin and sick little dog; she too came across the pear tree packed with caterpillars, the muddy dry and neglected well, the unplastered oven nearly falling apart; but when the little dog, and the pear tree, and the well, and the oven begged her to care for them, she answered them with spite and mockery: — Of course not! As if I would dirty the dear little hands of dear daddy and dear mummy! Have you had many servants like me? Then all of them, knowing that it would be easier to get milk from a barren cow than to put a spoiled and lazy girl in your debt, let her continue on her way in peace and asked nothing more from her. And walking straight ahead, she eventually reached Holy Sunday too; but here too she behaved surly, rudely and foolishly. Instead of making good and proper food and washing Holy Sunday's children as well as the old man's daughter had washed them, she scalded them all, so they cried and ran about crazed with stinging and pain. Then she made the food smoky, burned and tasteless, so that no one could put it in their mouth... and when Holy Sunday came from church, she put her hands on her head at what she found at home. But Holy Sunday, gentle and patient, did not want to trouble herself with such a scatterbrain and lazy girl; instead she told her to go up into the attic, choose whatever chest pleased her and go with God's blessing. The girl then went up and chose the newest and most beautiful chest; for she liked to take as much as possible and whatever was best and most beautiful, but she did not like doing good work. Then, as she came down from the attic with the chest, she did not even go to say goodbye and receive the blessing of Holy Sunday, but set off as if from an abandoned house and kept walking ahead; and she walked so fast her heels were cracking, for fear that Holy Sunday might change her mind and come after her, catch her and take back the chest. And when she arrived at the oven, beautiful pastries were in it! But when she approached to take some and satisfy her appetite, the fire burned her and she could not take any. At the well, the same: the little silver cups were there, no doubt, and the well was full of water to the brim; but when the girl wanted to put her hand on the cup and take water, the cups immediately sank, the water in the well dried up in an instant, and the girl dried up from thirst! When she passed the pear tree, there was no doubt it seemed beaten with a shovel from the many pears it had, but do you think the girl got to taste even one? No, for the pear tree had become a thousand times taller than it had been, its branches reaching into the clouds! And then... pick your teeth, old woman's daughter! Walking further, she met the little dog too; the necklace of gold coins was still around her neck; but when the girl wanted to take it, the little dog bit her and tore her fingers and did not let her lay a hand on it. Now the girl was biting her dear little fingers from spite and shame, but there was nothing to be done. Finally, with great difficulty she arrived home too, at her mother's, but even here the riches did not agree with them. For opening the chest, a multitude of dragons came out of it and immediately devoured the old woman, daughter and all, as if they had never existed in this world, and then the dragons vanished along with the chest. And the old man was left in peace from the old woman and had countless riches: he gave his daughter in marriage to a good and hardworking man. The roosters now crowed on the gate posts, on the doorstep and everywhere; while the hens no longer crowed like roosters in the old man's house, making trouble; for then they would not have had many days left either. Only this much remained: that the old man was left bald and hunchbacked from how much the old woman had stroked his head and tested his back with the fire poker to see if the cornbread was baked.

title: Cunning Iliana
text_english: Once upon a time something happened. If it had not happened, it would not be told. There was once an emperor who had three daughters; the oldest was beautiful, the middle one more beautiful, but the youngest, Ileane, was so fair that even the sun stopped to gaze at her and admire her charms. One day the emperor received the news that his neighbor, a mighty monarch, was no longer friendly, but wanted to fight with him on account of a great imperial feud. The emperor consulted the old men of the country, and, seeing there was nothing else to be done, he commanded his valiant soldiers to mount their horses, take their weapons, and prepare for the terrible battle which was to be fought. Before mounting himself, the emperor called his daughters, addressed a few fatherly, touching words to them, and gave each one a beautiful flower, a merry little bird, and a rosy-cheeked apple. "Whoever has her flower wither, her bird mope or her apple rot, I shall know has not kept her faith,"said the wise emperor; then mounting his steed he wished them "Good-health" and set off with his brave soldiers on their toilsome way. When the neighboring emperor's three sons heard the news that the emperor had quitted his home and gone to the war, they made an agreement among themselves and sprang on their horses to ride to the palace and vex the monarch by making his three daughters faithless to his trust. The oldest prince, a brave, spirited, handsome fellow, went first to see how matters stood and bring tidings afterward to the others. Three days and three nights the champion stood under the wall, but not one of the girls had appeared at the windows. In the gray dawn of the fourth day he lost patience, plucked up his courage, and tapped on the oldest princess's window. "What is it—what is it? What is wanted?" asked the royal maiden, roused from her sleep. "It is I, little sister," said the prince,"I, an emperor's son, who have stood under your window three days for love of you." The princess did not even approach the window, but replied in a prudent tone: "Go back home by the way you came; may flowers spring up before you and thorns remain behind." After three more days and nights the prince again knocked on the girl's window. This time the princess approached it, and said in a more gentle voice: "I told you to go back home by the way you came; may thorns spring up before you and flowers remain behind." Once more the prince waited three days and three nights under the maiden's window. In the gray dawn of the tenth day, that is after thrice three days and thrice three nights had passed, he smoothed his hair and for the third time tapped on the window. "What is it? Who is it? What is wanted?" asked the princess, this time somewhat more sternly than before. "It is I, little sister," said the prince. "For thrice three days I have stood longingly under your window. I would like to see your face, gaze into your eyes, and watch the words flow from your lips!" The princess opened the window, glanced angrily at the handsome youth, and said in a scarcely audible voice: "I would willingly look into your face and say a word or two to you, but first go to my younger sister—then come to me." "I'll send my younger brother," replied the prince. "But give me one kiss to make my way home pleasanter." And almost before he had spoken, he snatched a kiss from the beautiful girl. "May no second one fall to your lot," said the princess, wiping her mouth with her embroidered sleeve. "Go back home by the way you came; may flowers spring up before you and flowers remain behind." The prince went back to his brothers and told them all that had happened, and the second took his departure. After this prince had stood under the second princess's window nine times nine days and nine times nine nights and tapped for the ninth time at her window, she opened it and said to him kindly: "I would like to look at you and say a word or two to you, but first go to my youngest sister, then come to me." "I'll send my youngest brother," said the prince. "But give me one kiss, that I may hurry the faster." He had scarcely said it, when he stole a kiss. "May no second one fall to your lot," said this royal maiden too. "Go back home by the way you came, may flowers spring up before you and flowers remain behind!" The prince returned to his brothers, told them all that had happened, and—for the third time—a hero departed, the youngest son. When he reached the palace where the three sisters lived Ileane was standing at the window, and when she saw him, said merrily: "You handsome champion with the royal face, where are you hurrying, that you urge on your steed so hotly?" When the prince saw Ileane's face and heard Ileane's words, he stopped, gazed at her, and answered boldly: "I'm hurrying to the sun to steal one of its rays, to give to its sister and take her home, where she shall become my bride. Now, little sister, I will stop on my way to look at you, gaze at the radiance of your face, say a word to you and steal a word in reply." Ileane cleverly answered: "If your nature is like your words, if your soul is like your face, proud and beautiful, and mild and gentle, I will gladly call you into the house, seat you at a banquet, give you food and drink and kisses." The prince sprang from his horse as he heard these words, and answered boldly: "My nature will be like my speech, my heart like my face; let me in, seat me at the banquet, you shall never repent it from dawn till nightfall." He had scarcely uttered the words when he leaped upon the window-sill, jumped through the window into the room, went through the room to the table, and took his place at the very top, where the emperor had sat when he was a bridegroom. "Stop, stop!" said Ileane. "First let me see whether you are what you ought to be, and then we'll talk and begin our love-making. Can you make roses grow on burdocks?" "No!" said the prince. "Then the thistle is your flower," said clever Ileane. "Can you make the bat sing in a sweet voice?" "No!" said the prince. "Then night is your day," said clever Ileane. "Can you make apples grow on wolf's-bane?" "That I can!" said the prince. "Then that shall be your fruit!" replied the beautiful and cunning Ileane. "Sit down at the table." The prince took his place. Ah! but Ileane was indeed cunning Ileane. Ere he had fairly seated himself, he dropped, chair and all, into the deep cellar where the emperor's treasures were kept. Ileane now began to scream: "Help!" and when all the servants came rushing in to see what had happened, she told them she had heard a noise and was afraid that some one had got into the cellar to rob the emperor of his treasures. The servants did not waste many words, but instantly opened the iron door and went into the cellar, where they found the prince and brought him in disgrace to be sentenced. Ileane pronounced judgment. Twelve girls under punishment for some offense were to carry him out of the country, and when they had reached the frontier with him, each one was to give him a kiss. The order was obeyed. When the prince reached home and joined his brothers, he told them the whole story, and after every thing had been related their hearts were filled with rage. So they sent word to the two older princesses that they must arrange to have Ileane go to the three princes' court, so that they might revenge themselves upon her for the insult she had offered them. When the oldest daughter received this message from the prince she pretended to be sick, called Ileane to her bedside, and told her that she could not get well unless Ileane brought her something to eat from the princes' kitchen. Ileane would have done any thing for her sister's sake, so she took a little jug and set off for the court of the three princes, to beg or steal. When she reached the palace, she rushed breathlessly into the kitchen and said to the head-cook: "For heaven's sake, don't you hear the emperor calling you? Make haste, and see what is the matter." The cook took to his heels and ran as fast as he could, as though he had received an imperial command. Ileane, left alone in the kitchen, filled her jug with food, emptied all the dainty dishes that were on the fire upon the floor, and went away. When the princes heard of this insult they were still more enraged than before, sent another message to the two sisters and again prepared a revenge. As soon as the second sister received the news, she, too, pretended to be ill, called Ileane to her bed, and told her that she could not get well unless she tasted the wine in the princes' cellar. Ileane would have done any thing for her sister, so she took the little jug and prepared to go again. When she reached the court she rushed into the cellar, and, panting for breath, said to the head-butler: "For heaven's sake, don't you hear the emperor calling you? Make haste and see what is the matter." The butler took to his heels and ran as if he had received an imperial command. Ileane filled her jug with wine, poured out the rest on the cellar floor, and then hurried home. The princes sent a third message to the two princesses and told them they must send Ileane in a different way from what they had done before. This time both the princesses feigned illness, called their sister to them, and told her that they could not get well unless Ileane brought them two of the princes' apples. "My dear sisters," replied Ileane,"I would go through fire and water for you, how much more willingly to the princes." Taking the little jug she set off to find, seize, and bring back the fruit and save her dear sisters' lives. When the youngest prince learned that Ileane was coming to the garden to steal the golden apples, he gave orders that, if groans were heard there, nobody must dare go in, but let the person who was wailing, moan in peace. Then he hid huge knives, swords, spears, and many other things in the earth under the tree that bore the golden apples, concealing them so that only the sharp points rose out of the ground. After he had finished, he hid himself in a clump of bushes and waited for Ileane. She came to the gate, and seeing the two huge lions that kept guard there flung each of them a piece of meat; the lions began to tear it, and the princess went to the apple tree, stepped cautiously between the knives, swords, spears, and other things, and climbed into it. "May this do you much good, little sister," said the prince. "I'm glad to see you in my garden." "The pleasure is mine," replied Ileane,"since I have so brave and handsome a prince for my companion.
