He could not understand how to make his income meet his expenses. Then his younger son came timidly into the room. He placed the electricity and gas bills before him and whispered, "Father, please bring me something from the market today." Āhad looked once at his son and once at the utility bills. When he saw those bills, sweat broke out over his body, as if the roof of the house were now collapsing onto him. He was about to go out quickly when another news item flashed. At a press conference, the finance minister was blaming the present excessive price rises on the global market. He was saying, "The IMF loan will be available very soon. Be patient, people. We are now coming out of the crisis." Āhad switched off the television and stepped outside. In a short time, the state of the house had changed. Where there had once been contentment and ease, there were now anxiety and worry. Disagreements were rising over every matter. At the office too, Āhad argued with everyone about everything. He was worried about his sisters growing older and about the future of his children, but no solution came to his mind. After he paid the electricity and gas bills, his pockets were empty. As he came home with empty pockets, he took a black plastic bag out of his pocket on the way. As usual, he stopped at a restaurant and then returned home. When he entered the street, he went into his house, angrily muttering to himself. His younger son came running and snatched the black plastic bag from his hand. He ran to his grandfather and said happily, "Look, Grandpa, see how much Father has brought for me!" Āhad stepped forward and tried to take the plastic bag back from his son. At that moment the bag tore, and pieces of dry bread fell out of it and scattered everywhere.

title: Price of Dreams
text_english: To understand life, and to understand something from life, are two separate things. Many times we confuse the two. Because of this, a person may act in great haste. When our wishes remain unfulfilled, when the hopes attached to our dreams come to nothing, we are left bewildered. To whom should we turn with our questions? Should we ask God? Should we ask God's creatures? Should we ask this society, this order, or should we ask ourselves? When Aslam looked at his life from every side, everyone else appeared better off, more comfortable, and happier than he was. Lālā sat in the square with his cobbler's tools until evening and carried food home for his children. Uncle Hazūr kept his vegetable business going with only a few kinds of produce. Rājā the washerman, iron in hand, listened to Murad Parkoi's songs, smoked a cigarette, and laughed. In one corner of the square, Sharīf the barber, with a pair of scissors, a mirror, and the help of his three sons, had built the first cement house in their alley. Aslam pulled his M.A. degree out of a cloth bag and muttered to himself, speaking to the diploma: "If I had not obeyed your demands, I too would have become some master earning a little money from these circumstances." In that hard age, there was nothing in Aslam's hands. Rājā, fulfilling the duty of friendship, advised him: "Bring a chole [spiced chickpea] cart and set it beside my shop. By evening you could earn a hundred or two hundred rupees." Aslam was satisfied with the idea, but his mother did not accept it. "My son has studied so much," she said. "I want to make him a great babu [educated clerk], not a seller of chole." One day Aslam saw job advertisements in the newspaper. He quickly took his degrees and set off toward the Secretariat. He submitted applications for three posts. Now he was hopeful that he would get a job. He had received such good marks. He had worked so hard. His parents' prayers were with him. Thinking these thoughts, Aslam reached the Secretariat. As he wandered here and there, he saw Imdād, who took him to the canteen for tea. After listening to Aslam, Imdād laughed and said, "My friend, what world are you living in? This is not an age in which rights, justice, or hard work are enough to gain anything. This is only the age of money and wealth. As people say, 'The one who has property and resources is the one who is encouraged.'" Aslam swallowed a sip of hot tea and asked Imdād, "Then what should I do? Where should I go? Do something for me." Imdād said, "I will distribute five or ten thousand here and there for you." With his foolish laugh, Imdād placed before Aslam a price list for posts. Then he stood up to pay for Aslam's tea. Aslam came out resolved to arrange three lakhs [hundreds of thousands of rupees], fixing his eyes only on the office posts listed there. Time had placed Aslam in a trial. Now he could think of nothing except securing a government job. He wanted to buy an office post in the hope that later there would be promotion. Thinking of the three lakhs, he returned home. His mother gave him her gold bangles. His father sold his bicycle. By borrowing from place after place, Aslam completed the amount of three lakhs. With Imdād's help, he handed the money to the man who had promised him a job. That man told Aslam to come back in two days. Aslam returned home full of happiness. His parents thanked God. Now Aslam began counting every minute. The next morning, as he crossed the square, he gave no thought to the cobbler, the washerman, or the uncle who sold vegetables. At Sharīf the barber's shop, he looked at himself in the large mirror, had his beard and moustache tidied, and picked up that day's newspaper. When he read the large headline, darkness spread before his eyes. His head began to spin. He leaned against a wall for support. Then he read the news again: "Imdād and Rozi Khān, who deceived people out of lakhs of rupees in the name of employment, have fled abroad with their associates." Aslam felt as if the mirror in Sharīf the barber's shop had shattered into pieces and fallen upon his head.

title: The Miraculous Man
text_english: Morning had come. The dogs and cats stretched themselves. A few steps apart from one another, they settled into their places, facing east. From a distance a man was approaching on a bicycle. Then the eyes of the dogs and cats, which had been closed in drowsiness, opened one after another. They wagged their tails and stood up. They watched in the direction from which the man was coming. It was like a person whose blood pressure has fallen, who opens his eyes at the sight of food. At last the man reached the dogs sitting in the front row. Wagging their tails, the dogs greeted him. They pressed themselves against his legs. The man untied the cloth bag hanging from the handle of his bicycle. From inside it he took out a plastic bag. Then he scattered a heap of chicken feet before them, because offal meat had become expensive. People who kept fine dogs bought it and took it away; that was why he brought chicken feet instead. The cats waited for their turn, wondering when the master would turn his face toward them. A few cats appealed to him too, crying, "Meow, meow." At last the man walked his bicycle toward the cats. They too pressed against his legs, their tails raised and waving before him. From the other handle of the bicycle, the man opened the second bag and scattered chicken feet in front of them in the same way. Chicken feet were hard for cats to chew, but when hunger comes to a human being or an animal, it makes them chew even the hardest things. In time, the people of the villages and towns began to call this man "the miraculous man." Just as friends and enemies sit together as companions when driven by hunger, so these dogs and cats gradually became friends. The people's faith in the miraculous man grew stronger. How did the dogs and cats know that the master was coming? The dogs and cats ate together. The dogs and cats sat together at the master's feet. After some time, this man died. His funeral was held there. The cats and dogs, sorrowful, attended the funeral together. From then on, when people passed that way, they bought offal meat and brought it for the dogs and cats, in order to please the spirit of the miraculous man. Dogs and cats from near and far also smelled the meat and came. Then some of the dogs and cats became pregnant and began giving birth to puppies and kittens. Growing up together, the puppies and kittens played like brothers and sisters. People's reverence for the miraculous man grew still stronger. A roof was put over his grave. Some men became faqirs [ascetic devotees]. The pestle and mortar, the hemp drink, and the smell of hashish drew young men there. Cocaine entered among them too. Addicts sat at the feet of men who came to the tomb, just as dogs and cats sat there. People outside, who did not know the story, became even more astonished: the boundaries between dogs, cats, and humans had disappeared. Dogs were no longer enemies of cats, nor were dogs called mad animals for humans. Then whatever beauty belongs to a royal court began to flourish there day by day. In the midst of this, a great unrest broke out and a curfew was imposed in the city. The movement of people stopped. For a few days, the dogs, the cats, and the people present at the tomb held a faint hope that people would begin moving about again. But nothing happened. The curfew was extended. Now the dogs began, one by one, to growl and bark at one another and at the cats. People behaved toward them in the same way. First the cats began to leave, one by one. After that the men grew weary. Fearing that the dogs might become mad, they abandoned the place. Finally the dogs too wandered far away from the tomb in search of food. Then came rain and snowfall. Wind blew. Dust storms rose. The remains of the banners were carried away. The earthen room built at the head of the tomb collapsed. After some time the rain washed away its mud. At last army vehicles began to pass over it. The ground became level, just as it had been at the beginning. No trace or sign of the tomb remained. There was no indication of the place where humans, cats, dogs, and cocaine addicts had gathered and made a shrine. Where had they found a miraculous man? Later it became known that near the old tomb a large market had been made: a market for foreigners to eat dog meat, for cats to be tamed, and for cocaine addicts to sell their kidneys.

title: Traveler
text_english: When the tribe of Chief Ādal Khān was traveling toward Nārī by way of Bolān, he halted the tribe on the grounds of Bībī Nānī late in the afternoon so they might spend the night there. Evening had settled. While the women were busy preparing the evening meal, the children of the tribe had gone down into the riverbed to visit Bībī Nānī's tomb. They came back panting. They told Ādal Khān, "We saw Shae Mured! He was standing beside Bībī Nānī's tomb." Chief Ādal Khān set out in that direction with a few other men. Beside the head of Bībī Nānī's tomb stood a white-bearded man. The chief came near him and called out, "Sir, who are you?" The man said, "Today I am your guest." The chief stepped forward and greeted the old man. Then he took the old man with him, and they walked back to where the tribesmen were waiting. As on every night, the evening gathering around Chief Ādal Khān had begun. The children and the women of the tribe too had assembled to see the guest who had come among them. The chief consulted his companions about asking the guest who he was. Then he turned to the guest and said, "Sir, who are you? Honored elder, please tell us your story." The old man looked once around the gathering. Then he began to speak slowly. "Chief, this is a story from thirty years ago. I was in the Marri country. I do not remember the first battle of the Marri, but I remember clearly their second battle, which they fought against the British. I was a very young boy when, one night, I became the guest of a Marri family. The old and the young of that family were sitting around a great fire. They were roasting meat. The young men were sharpening their swords. The elders were loading their muzzle-loading rifles. The women and children of the family, seated apart, were singing war songs and clapping their hands. In short, every person was full of spirit. That fervor continued all night. I did not understand what it was all about. Around me there was no clue to the reason for that night's gathering. In the morning, I could not find a single person in the family's hamlet. After a while, an old woman brought me bread, butter, and sour milk. I asked her, 'Where have your men gone?' The old woman looked into my eyes, and then she said, 'My son, at first the British occupied our Marri Kohistan by force. The Marri fought then too, but the other Baloch did not support them. The Marri have not forgotten the looting and plunder of the British. After so many years, today the Marri have again prepared themselves to fight the British. This time the Marri are gathering in every valley and at every campsite of Marri Kohistan. They are fighting for the land of their fathers and grandfathers.' When I heard this, I left my meal. I took a blunt sword in my hand and stood up. The old woman looked at me closely, very closely, and then said, 'My son, I know you are a Baloch. The honor of your forefathers is still alive in you. But listen carefully: the decision of this battle cannot be made here alone in the Kohistan of the Marri. Once before the Marri let themselves be killed. They were killed because the other Baloch did not give them help. Today too the Marri stand alone. There is no gain in the Marri always giving their heads in sacrifice. My son, listen to my words. Leave here at once. Give news to all the Baloch of the country: the Marri have risen again to spill the blood of their young and their elders on their own land. If there is honor in the Baloch nation, let them fight the British everywhere. My son, I hold out my hem to you and implore you. Carry my message, the message of this old woman, to every corner of the country.' The brave woman kissed my head and gave me leave. Chief, thirty years have passed since that day. In all this time I have not returned to my own home. Across this country, from house to house and from tent to tent, I have carried the message of that brave woman. I went straight to the Iranian Baloch on the other side of our land and delivered the message to them too. I have heard the sound of the rifle of Jīand the Fighter. I have seen him battle the British like a lion. In Jhalawan I also became the friend of the martyr Nūrā. With my own hands I washed the wounds on his body. Chief, the British took Marri lives. Jīand died in prison. They made Nūrā a martyr. They confined the Khān of the Baloch in Pishin. They rampaged through the four corners of the land. Yet I am still alive. To this day, it remains my duty to carry the message of the brave Marri woman." When he had told this story, the old man stood up. While everyone was still watching him, the old man disappeared into the darkness of the night.

title: Doctor
text_english: The cold wind from the north cut like a sword. It was impossible even to put a foot on the ground. The pits, holes, grass, and shrubs along the road were frozen in snow. Sahtī's single thin shawl was wet too. The bullets of the north wind pierced through its patches and numbed her body. Her bare feet had swollen from the cold. Her fingernails had turned blue. Her tears rolled down like hailstones. The cold made her tongue stammer. Her hands had lost their strength. On top of a bull, her husband was wrapped in an old blanket like a ball of thread. At one moment he rolled to one side, and at the next he rolled to the other. The woman raised that dry log of a man, Basshām, this way and then pulled him that way. Struggling to keep him upright, she made her way to the doctor's place. Many cars were parked in front of the doctor's clinic, and many more were arriving. The noise of the cars made the woman lose her senses. Her bull was frightened and bewildered. Her grip slipped from the blanket. Her husband toppled from the bull and fell onto the frozen snow. "Alas!" he cried out, and fainted. The bull leapt away in panic, whipping its tail against its back because of the honking vehicles. It ran and reached its stable in a single breath. Crying and slapping her own face, Sahtī gathered Basshām to herself. She placed his head on her knee and wiped the blood from his mouth and nose. Then she tore a strip from her shawl, made a knot, and tied his shoulder. Her son, fallen from the baby sling, was writhing in the middle of the road like one seized by unbearable pain. Basshām's gasping and the sobbing of the child wounded Sahtī's soul. Her shawl had fallen to one side. The cold of the north wind no longer affected her, nor did her body seem aware of it. The honking of the cars was melting the brain in her head. A long line of vehicles had stopped there. The drivers kept sounding their horns, urging her to remove the body from the road. Sahtī was overcome. She wondered how she could lift Basshām's body from the road and how she could comfort the child. When she looked toward the vehicles for help, the drivers shouted abuse at her from where they sat. "Lift your half-dead man quickly!" For one moment the woman looked at the child, and for the next she looked into Basshām's eyes. Her tears had run dry. Inside her, her mind flared up. She was astonished by her own helplessness. What could she do? Then a fat man wrapped in a felt coat stepped out of one of the cars. He came up to Sahtī and scolded her. He grabbed Basshām by the legs and dragged him off the road. He said, "Can you not see our boss? He has caught cold. And you are blocking the road. You are holding up everyone and everything. Pick up your child, or he will be crushed to pieces beneath the tires of the cars and stick to the snow." After he said this, the line of vehicles began to move. Sahtī moved quickly. She picked up her child and brought him to Basshām's side. Basshām was already weak. He had long been suffering from cough and cold. But the fall onto the snow and the dragging brought him close to death. Sahtī uncovered the child. He too had caught the cold. His hands and feet were numb. His eyes and mouth were shut. Sahtī lifted the child and placed him beside Basshām. Then she rushed inside and cried before the doctor, "Sir, my husband is critically ill outside. Please tell your staff to lift him from the snow and the north wind and bring him in here." The doctor did not listen to her. One of those sitting in the waiting area answered instead: "Ignore her. She is mad. She settled on the road with her family and stayed there all day. She made us and our bosses wait in the snow and cold for ten minutes." Sahtī lamented, wept, and pleaded, "Please, doctor, for God's sake. I am destitute. My bull has run away. My child has died of the cold. My husband has been suffering from cough and cold, and he too is on the edge of death. I have no one else and no support. If he dies, how will I live? You are a doctor for everyone. Rich or poor, we are equal before you. I am a poor, powerless, helpless woman. I cannot lift my husband and bring him here. I beg you, for the sake of your own children, send someone to bring my husband inside. Examine him and give him medicine." Hearing the woman's words, all those sitting by the fire frowned. The doctor's face too became hard. He said, "God made you poor. I did not make you poor. Go and take your complaints about your poverty to your God. Besides, I have no staff to lift your stinking husband and bring him here. You make yourself blind and do not see: many wealthy, respectable, honorable people are sitting here. They will not become your laborers. Go and sit outside. When I have finished with the rich people and the others, I will speak to you." Sahtī had not expected this from the doctor: that he would remain indifferent to the death of her child, to her husband's nearness to death, to the winter snow, to those lying outside in the cold, and that he would not help a powerless woman. The doctor's words settled in Sahtī's mind like a skewer reddened in fire. She struck herself against the wall and cried aloud, "For God's sake! The sick man lying in the snow is human, just as you are. If anyone saw even a dog in such torment, his heart would move with pity. But you people!" Sahtī began to tremble. The doctor's staff took her by the arms and dragged her outside. Her shawl was left behind in the doctor's office. From crying, lamenting, and struggling to hold her husband, her hair had spread over her face like threads. The cord of her collar had torn loose from her shirt. From lamenting and striking her own face, her face was bruised. From grief and sorrow, her eyes were swollen. Now she was shedding only bloody tears. But she was unaware of her own condition. Once more she rushed toward the doctor. As soon as she entered, she fell at the doctor's feet. She said, "God has taken my child. My last hope is my husband. His life is in God's hands, but because of your lack of mercy, perhaps he too is dying and leaving me alone. I ask nothing more now. Only have someone lift him from the snow and put him under shelter." The doctor answered again, "Sit beside your husband. After I have seen the gentlemen, I will give him some treatment." When Sahtī tried to plead further, the doctor's staff pushed her, took her even out of the courtyard, and left her there. Sahtī lost every hope she had placed in the doctor. She rushed to her husband and uncovered his face, perhaps thinking he might revive by himself, perhaps thinking he might still seek shelter. But when she saw her husband, her soul and body seemed to separate, for now he lay motionless beside the body of their child. He was at rest forever. He was free now from the need for the doctor's medicine or any shelter from the cold. The grief and worries of her earlier trials had nearly driven Sahtī mad. The corpses of her child and her husband robbed her of clarity and sense. From the beginning Sahtī had no other protector. With their deaths, she was released from all the troubles, problems, sorrows, and worries of this world. Crying "Doctor, doctor," she ran away, far from those people, wanting to distance herself from humanity itself.

title: Prisoners of Love
text_english: On a winter morning, the cold of the north wind carried the message that the leaves had begun to fall. The scattering of leaves everywhere also signaled that spring had migrated from that place. As on every day, I sat on that bench waiting for you. Suddenly I felt the touch of your cold, soft hands on my face. I covered your hands with my own. There you were, standing before me with your beautiful smile. Your gentle smile seemed to be kissing the hands of the small clouds spread across the sky. I said, "You are late again today." You answered, "Hush," and smiled again. After that, I said nothing. You took my hands and made me stand. We walked over the dry leaves, looking at one another and speaking softly. In the rustling of the leaves there was a sorrowful, quiet melody. You said, "Sometimes society crushes people's desires the way we are trampling these dry leaves without mercy." I said, "Human beings are truly the most self-centered creatures in the universe. I have met many people who claimed to be principled, but when their own business and interest came into question, they forgot every principle." You said, "Along with that, these dry fallen leaves carry another message: human beings hold their beauty and value only as long as they remain attached to the branch of the tree of life. When someone plucks the leaf from that tree, it becomes useless, just like these leaves." Agreeing with your words, I said, "These leaves also tell us that after every rise comes a decline." You said, "Sometimes green leaves also fall from a branch." I said, "Indeed. Such leaves are taken away by sudden hardship and misfortune, just as a strong gust of wind carries leaves away. If they are firmly rooted, the wind cannot blow them off; otherwise..." While we were speaking, the wind suddenly became violent. It swept us both from our feet and lifted us into the air. We drifted through the sky together with a flock of birds flying in the clouds, free from every sorrow. They flew in their own way, wherever their hearts wished to go. They perched wherever their hearts wished to perch. When you saw those birds, you said to me, "Perhaps it would have been better if we had been birds instead of humans." I did not agree, but to encourage you I said, "Maybe." Wrinkles gathered on your forehead and you said, "I truly dislike that 'maybe.'" Then, along with the birds, we came down into a garden full of spring, full of colors and fragrance. I was bewildered: how had we arrived from the season of falling leaves into spring? In that garden there were many kinds of flowers. Rain was falling over them. Butterflies carrying tiny lamps danced with each raindrop. A dance of lamps with raindrops‚ what a spectacle it was! There were many kinds of trees and many fruits. A stream was flowing. Birds and butterflies flew here and there, making a scene as beautiful as a rainbow. From somewhere a heart-watering melody came to our ears, like the sound of our mouth harp. You chased a butterfly. I followed you. The butterfly flew into a gathering of fairies. When the fairies saw you, they embraced you. They kissed your hands and cheeks. You were astonished. They said, "You are one of us. How did you find yourself among these beasts? Now we will never let you return to those beasts. Stay with us in our beautiful world. Here there are only flowers, spring, bright colors, rainbows, and soft clouds. We will play with stars, birds, and butterflies. Let us recite poetry. Let us make music and clap our hands. All the beauties of the world's beauties are present here. We possess every color. What do you people have? You do every act for show. Every action of yours is false. Even your smiles are no longer sincere. Your love is wrapped in the clothes of self-interest. Unlike your world, there is no anxiety here. No one fears another. Unlike your world, love is not blamed here. No one bears ill will toward anyone here. Everyone here is without worry. Everyone is free from grief." I raised my voice and said, "She is my beloved. I will not let you keep her. I will take her back." The fairies laughed at my words and said, "But do you humans even know love? Did you say all that only so you might escape from us fairies?" You said, "Let me go today. I will go and return." They said, "We will let you go on one condition: sing a song for us in your voice. We will all accompany your song with our melody. We will make an ensemble and a dance." You began to sing. The fairies began their melody. They began to dance. Then you too began to dance. Such an atmosphere arose that I felt the flowers, trees, colors and rainbows, scenes and clouds, soft clouds, moon and stars, lamps and lights were all dancing together with you. It was as if the entire universe were dancing. With that dance, a special rapture came over you, and you drifted into a trance with the fairies. Fear seized me that you might forget me. You blended into their ensemble. I began to suspect that you too were one of the fairies. The melodies were spreading such intoxication. At that moment, the sound of someone's footsteps brought me back from that state of mind to reality. I looked around. Neither you nor those scenes remained. There was only that dark cell in which I had been imprisoned for the past thirty years. My hands and feet were tightly bound in chains. And then I noticed that you too were a prisoner, bound in the same kind of chains, in a cell on the other side.

title: Ganjān
text_english: It was dawn. The sun was about to rise. The stars in the sky had hidden themselves, making way for the light of the sun. Wrapped inside her blankets, Ganjān was searching for a sweet dream in deep sleep. Her dreams were modest. All her wealth was the hollow of that land. In her beautiful gidan [nomadic tent] in that hollow, besides two camels for migration, she had goats, a water bag, a milk bag, carpets, decorative rugs, and a handmill. In that hollow there was also fresh, life-giving air. Her mother's affectionate voice echoed through the beautiful mountain basin: "Ganjān! Mistress of my treasures. Mistress of my fortune. Get up, essence of my life. Morning has come." Ganjān opened her eyes in a pampered way. As her mother improvised a song with her name, she rose, still swaying with sleep. She untied the string of the water bag and drank water. She cupped water in her hands and washed her face. Her mother called out, "Ganjān, do not waste too much water. You know that although we are not without water, we bring it from a great distance. And usually you are the one who brings it." A smile spread over Ganjān's face, and she stretched herself. Looking up at the sky, she said, "Mother, if God were merciful to us, fountains and springs would flow more plentifully. I will go and bring water." Ganjān's name meant one who becomes mistress of treasures. Fortune had fallen into her lap when, at her birth, people announced the end of a long drought of seven years. Abundance spread across that plateau and basin. Because of that timely rain, the abundance was taken as an auspicious sign of her good fortune. Now they had Ganjān. Wherever they migrated with her and settled, success kissed their feet. She was now in her fifteenth year. Each year the heavens blessed the earth with gifts and made it fertile. From the breasts of the grasses and shrubs of the basin, which fed them well and bore fruit year after year, milk seemed to drip. The beauty of the mountains increased even more. The fragrance of grass and shrubs, carried by the wind, gave the message of nature's loves. The springs and fountains took pride in their water. Now Ganjān's land shone with abundant joy and happiness. Her land appeared the most beautiful in the whole area. At every turn there were joys, happiness, and attractions. Nature had given that land so much that only the gifts visible to nature itself could be seen by people. Beneath her feet there was even more abundance than that, hidden in the ground. Ganjān was untouched by worldly interest and desire, free from the noises of new luxurious machines. Not even the wind of the age touched her. How could she know that she truly was mistress of treasures? Neighboring eyes watched that land closely. Ganjān drank a cup of tea. She lifted the curtain wall of the gidan. She cleaned inside and outside the tent. She poured water from the leather water bag into a small water bag and handed it to her father. Her father kissed her on the head. Then he herded the goats and led them out to graze. Ganjān hung the leather water bag around her neck, wrapped her shawl about her throat, and set out toward the spring by the mountain to fetch water. When she crossed the edge of the mountain, she lost her senses. Beside the mountain, tents had been pitched. In the middle of the tents stood a large group of men. All their faces were covered with masks. Some people were trying to run away, but officers were working hard to catch them. The red lights flashing on top of their vehicles, together with their sirens, tore the sky. It was as if a battle had broken out. Covered by a cloud of fear, the sound of gunshots spread. A cry of "Ouch!" rang out. For a few moments, Ganjān stood motionless. The scene astonished her. On one side were the beauty of the mountains, the chirping of birds, the swaying of the shampastir [local grass]; on the other side were the shouts of men. Thinking, she took a few steps forward toward the spring. From ahead, men shouted, "Stay back, girl. What are you doing here? Leave at once, otherwise you too will be quarantined here." With trembling lips she said, "Why our spring, our water? From where will we get water?" "You want to drink this water? Impossible. Get out of here. Is this your grandfather's spring? The whole area is contaminated with cholera. Run away from here at once. Do not come this way again even by mistake, or you too will catch cholera." These words filled Ganjān with fear and anxiety. Putting the end of her shawl into her mouth, she ran back toward her gidan, tripping and stumbling. Along the way, she lost her sandals among the rocks. Her feet became bloody and bruised. At last, breathless, she reached the tent. When her mother saw her distress, she rushed out of the gidan. She took Ganjān in her arms, thinking that some wild animal must have chased her daughter. For some time she held her close to her breast. When Ganjān's breathing calmed, her mother asked, "What happened, my dear?" Sweat dripped from Ganjān's forehead. For a moment she stared at her empty leather water bag. Then, with trembling lips, she said, "Oh Mother, our spring!" "Yes, what happened? Tell me, what happened to our spring? Have wild animals taken possession of it?" "Yes, you may say beasts have made an enclosure around it. Dangerous outsiders have set up a village of tents and settled there. They did not let me go to my spring. They said, 'Cholera has struck the whole area and the towns. We have made a quarantine zone here in the mountain basin, far from settlements, to isolate those affected by cholera so that it will not spread to others. It is for safety, for safety.' Our spring! Where will we get our water now? Our spring too has been contaminated by cholera." Ganjān's eyes filled with tears. Her tears rolled down. With a cold, sorrowful sigh, her mother said, "Oh Ganjān! We have faced so many hardships: drought, wolves, attacks by wild animals, and loss of livestock. Cholera fell upon us that night when they snatched your brother from his sound sleep in the darkness ten years ago. They abducted him. You were too young then, so you do not remember. He has been missing to this day. I wait for him every night." Hearing these words, Ganjān's body gave way. She fell to her knees. With quivering lips she whispered, "Brother, brother."

title: The King's Son
text_english: Once upon a time there was a king, and he had no children. In short, he went to a perfect faqir [holy mendicant], and the faqir asked Allah and performed some blowing and spiritual rites, and Allah granted that king a son. The son was very beautiful and of handsome appearance. Allah had given him such beauty that whoever in the world saw him would fall in love with him. When he grew young, proposals began to come from far and wide, from great people, saying that his marriage ought to take place with their daughter. In those very days, the same faqir also came to the king, the one through whose blowing and rites Allah had given him a son. The faqir heard talk of the prince's marriage and said to the king, "Your son's marriage will be with the daughter of the poor washerman who lives in the city." The washerman's daughter was blind in one eye and squint-eyed, and because of this no one would marry the poor girl. At this statement of the faqir, the king was overcome by great anger and said to the faqir, "Faqir sahib [respected faqir], if anyone else had said this to me, I would have had him put on the gallows." The faqir said to the king, "If you need your son's life, then accept my word and arrange his marriage with the washerman's daughter. If you do not do it, your son's wedding will be with death." On the faqir's saying, the king sent two men to the washerman's house with a marriage proposal, saying, "My little one will marry your little one." The washerman became very happy. But the king's minister became very angry with the king; rather, he turned against the king. After some days the wedding took place with great pomp and splendour, and along with it the king too was removed from the kingship. The king and his wife took their son and went and sat in the washerman's house. About eleven years passed after the marriage. In the eleventh year a child was born to the king's son. As soon as the child was born, light came into the child's mother's eyes, and with the coming of that light the world changed. The king became king again. One day the faqir came and said, "Now, for seven generations of yours, there will be kingship and only kingship." After that the king began to live a life of pleasure and comfort, and the line of his kingship continued afterwards as well.

title: The Mad King
text_english: Once upon a time there was a king who was very mad and foolish. In his kingdom there were often fights and quarrels. One day a man came into the king's court and said, "Long live the king, my house has collapsed, and there has been much loss." The king said, "Bring at once the man who built his house." The search was begun, and after much searching and inquiry the mason who had built the house was brought before the court. With great authority the king said to the mason, "What kind of house did you build for this poor man, that it collapsed?" The mason said, "Long live the king, it is not my fault. I was raising the wall of the house when a beautiful young woman, adorned with necklace and ornaments, passed by the house. I kept looking at her, and the brick was set wrongly; because of that the house collapsed." The king gave the order, "Bring that young woman at once." The servants brought the young woman into the court, and the king said to her, "Shameless woman, are you not ashamed? You walk about adorned with ornaments, and people look at you and go mad?" The young woman answered, "Long live the king, it is not my fault. All this fault belongs to the goldsmith who made this necklace. If the goldsmith had not made the necklace, I would not have put it around my neck; then the mason would not have made a mistake, and that poor man's house would not have collapsed." Hearing the young woman's answer, the king flared up as if a fire had been lit in him, and in anger he said, "Take this young woman away and put her on the gallows." When the young woman heard this order of the king, she became very frightened, and, escaping the servants' notice, she ran away. The servants went and said to the king, "Long live the king, the young woman has run away." The king said, "It is no matter. If the young woman has run away, what of it? Put someone else on the gallows." The servant came outside, and what should he see but two faqirs walking along the road. They went and seized one faqir. The second faqir, who was with him, asked, "Where are you taking him?" The servant said, "It is the king's order that he is to be put on the gallows." The second faqir said, "Friend, do not worry. I shall also go with you. But do one thing: at the time when they are about to put you on the gallows, you should say, 'I shall die,' and I shall say, 'No, I shall die.'" In short, in this way, at the time of being put on the gallows, a quarrel broke out between the two faqirs. One said, "I shall go to the gallows," and the other said, "I shall." The people became helpless and went and said to the king, "Long live the king, a fierce quarrel is going on between those two faqirs. One says, 'I shall go to the gallows,' and the other says, 'No, I shall go.'" Hearing this, the king came himself, and, after arriving, said to those faqirs, "Tell me, what is the matter?" The faqirs said, "We know that the fortunate one who dies on this day will rule as king in the next world as well." As soon as the king heard this, he became happy and said, "Do not put anyone on the gallows; I myself shall go to the gallows." Saying this, the king ran and climbed onto the gallows. Now it is not known whether he rules as king in the next world or not.

title: Two Friends
text_english: Once upon a time there were two friends, and between them there was great love and affection. One of them was married, and the other placed the ceremonial turban on his head; now their friendship became still firmer. When he saw his friend's wife, she was very beautiful, and he changed his gaze toward her. After some time he said to his friend's wife, "I have fallen in love with you. So now what shall I do?" She was a very clever, wise, and honourable woman. She said to him, "Come to the rooftop this evening." The evil-minded friend came to the rooftop as soon as evening fell, and the woman said to her husband, "Enemies live around us; let us go and make a round on the rooftop." Her husband went to the rooftop, and what should he see but his friend sitting on the rooftop. He said to him, "O my friend, what are you doing here?" That faithless friend said, "A wager had been laid among us. Some people said such-and-such a roof is large, some said such-and-such is large, and I said, 'No, my friend's roof is larger than all of them.' Then I thought I should go and see my friend's roof and come back; that is why I had come here." The next day he again came to that woman and said, "Now what shall I do?" The woman said, "Come this evening near the stack of grass." The evil-minded friend went away; evening fell, and he went and sat near the grass stack. The woman said to her husband, "Today we must bring grass for the livestock ourselves." When he went near the stack to take out grass, what should he see ahead but his dear friend sitting there. He asked, "O my friend, what are you doing here?" That evil-minded friend replied, "Ah, what shall I do? Today in the village the thieves were taking counsel that they would hide away such-and-such person's grass. I thought, 'My friend has a great deal of livestock; if the grass is taken away, he will suffer loss.' That is why I came and sat guarding your stack." He heard this statement of his friend and thanked him truly and sincerely. On the third day he again came to that woman and said with great humility, "Do not deceive me. Now tell me, what should be done now?" The woman said, "Come this evening and sit inside the cattle shed, beside the bullock. Today I will surely come." The man, quietly and secretly, went before evening and sat inside the cattle shed by the bullock's manger. When evening came, the wife said to her husband, "Now the time of farming has come. Before sleeping at night, one should surely go and see the bullocks, to make sure they have not become thin or unwell. Go first and see the bullock." When he went inside among the animals, what should he see but the very same dear friend sitting beside the bullock. The friend's eyes fell on his friend, and he said, "O my friend, what are you doing here again today?" That evil-minded friend said, "Today a wager had been laid in the village about whose bullock in our settlement is strong. I said that my friend's bullock is strong. Then I thought I should first go and see my friend's bullock, in case I lose the wager; that is why I had come." He took him outside and said to his wife, "Make tea." The wife made tea. After giving tea to his friend, he said to his wife, "You saw how sympathetic my friend is." The wife said, "I know the sympathy of this poor fellow." Then she turned to her husband's friend and said, "O faithless one, are you my husband's sympathetic friend? Is this your friendship, that you look at me with an evil eye? O ill-intentioned man, I am your sister." That ill-intentioned man became water with shame; in front of his friend, his face too was blackened. What else could the poor man do? He was no longer able even to face them, and he had also lost the honour of a good friend.

title: Paharia Origin: A Myth
text_english:
As per Pahariā mythology, the first human was born after the gods. The imaginary world of the Pahariā was known as Indakup Bhuinghar — the underworld. Even the sunlight was inept at reaching there. After God's birth in that nether region, the first human to take birth in that sacred place was a Pahariā. Next to take birth were twelve brothers Dhani and sixteen sisters Rajā Devi. First of all, Budhārajā — the supreme god, took his birth in a place named Ambed Thāndar. He looked at the universe and found that nobody was ruling it. He took the whole universe as his kingdom and slept again. Two Pahariā brothers took birth in Ambed Bhandār. That place was located on the other side of seven oceans and sixteen rivers. These two men tried to cross the seven oceans and sixteen rivers but failed. They took help from a tortoise and a crocodile. The bank of the river they crossed is known as Baruka ghat. The two Pahariās were brothers since their origin was from one source. However, while crossing the river, they separated into two clans. The man who took help from the tortoise was known as Netam, and the brother who crossed the river with the help of the crocodile was known as Sodi. They became saga (kin) or bandhu kutum to expand their progeny and, thus, the Pahariā community originated on earth. Then the twelve brothers Rajdhani and sixteen sisters Rajdevi ruled over the earth. Meanwhile, there was a quarrel between Budhārajā and the Desdhani god Bhima. Bhima said, "I rule this land." Budhārajā said, "No. I am ruling the country, not you." They fought with each other, but could not

resolve it. There was a war between them. Finally, Bhima told Budhārajā, "It's better that you rule the subjects." Budhārajā took some water from the water-gourd and sprinkled it on the earth, but that was not sufficient for cultivation. The rain was patchy, and the farmers could not cultivate. So Budhārajā could not rule the earth. He left the rule. Subsequently, it was the turn of Bhima to rule, but he desired to end the epoch in a deluge. He also fixed a day to put an end to the whole creation of his time — Yuga. None but the fish, frog and waterborne creatures were aware of this flood. Meanwhile, a Pahariā woman had been there to fetch water from the pond. She found that the frog was playing the game of love with the fish and the fish was with the frog. The Pahariā woman asked them why they were involved in such an unethical act. They replied, "Don't you know that Desh Dhani Bhima has fixed a day for a deluge to end this earth. Better that you also go home and play the game of love with your husband." Listening to this, the Pahariā woman returned home hurriedly and requested her husband to come to her bed. The old Pahariā asked, "Surprisingly, for a long time, you have not called me for mating. What is the matter today?" She replied, "There will be a deluge, so the fish and frogs are mating with each other. Why not enjoy before we perish?" After listening to this, the old Pahariā man speculated that perhaps Desh Dhani Bhima had decided to end creation. So he made a boat from the Gambhari tree. He kept all the belongings like food, clothes, house, well, firewood in that boat so that their progeny could survive for another yuga. Before the day of the deluge, the Pahariā couple positioned their son and daughter in the boat and waited for the deluge. When Bhima opened his water-gourd, there was uninterrupted rain for seven days and seven nights. All the creatures on earth perished. Due to the flood, the subterranean water sources became an open land, and the land where the boat was docked became a mountain and upland. The boat floated on the water in the deluge for twelve years. One day Bhima wanted to listen to the voices of human beings. He was curious to know if some human beings were still alive after the deluge. So he created a crow from the dirt of his thigh. He ordered the crow to search for the existence of human beings. The crow searched for twelve years but did not find a human being. Tired, the crow sat on the boat and heard the feeble voice of a human on the boat. The crow informed Bhima about the presence of a human being. Bhima sent three gods — Inder, Lakha Rāi and Agin Rāi to dry the deluged water. After drying the water, Lakharai hit the boat with his axe. The axe bounced from the hand and hit his forehead. Desh Dhani promised that he would not destroy the earth anymore. He promised that he would end the deluge on earth on the day when the horse would bear horns.

God rescued these two brothers and their sister from the boat. He decided to teach the art of archery, cultivation, and production of food to these two. He also taught them the Pahariā language. Therefore, the language of the Pahariā is known as the language of God. The first few words that the Pahariā learnt from God are, sahaya bhandār (house), bajarmundiā (Raggi), beda fawa (paddy), bichhalmundi (masa — brihi), kadad got (bean), kanabin (koshla-millet), narmanja (human), dadukhanta (baby), ang (body), kantakhāi (sheep), sonarkhure (cow), sing bāhān (buffalo). The words they inherited from their supreme God are their world.

title: Rice from Heaven
text_english:
Almost all the residents of a village were impoverished. They tried cutting firewood. A couple lived in that village. The wife told her husband, "Everyone is cutting wood, you also go and cut wood." The husband cut the wood, collected it and prepared a dahi ‚Äì a shifting cultivation. He sowed paddy in that dahi. The paddy sprouted, grew up and gave an ample harvest. The paddy turned yellow and began to ripen. The man made a five feet high Mancha-pandal in the field to watch the paddy field and save it from the attack of wild animals. He watched over the paddy field till it was cut down. He did not even allow an ant to take away a grain of paddy. He decided to cut the paddy the next morning. He went home to get the ILA (paddy-cutter knife). That night he did not return to the field and stayed back home. That night the elephants came to that field and ate the paddy. In the morning the man came and found that there was no paddy in the area. He knew that the elephants had eaten it. He sat on a watch that night. He caught hold of the leg of an elephant. The elephant flew to heaven. The gods in heaven asked the elephant. "Why did you bring this man to this place?" The elephant said, "We ate his paddy, so he caught hold of our leg." The gods said to the elephant to feed him, and they gave him delicious food. The gods said, "Leave him in his place." The gods gave some rice in a bundle and said, "Take this rice. Cook the number of rice equal to the number of your family." Then the pata hati ‚Äì elephant leader, took the man from heaven and left him near the dahi. The man came back home and told his wife everything. They were only two members. So they cooked two grains of rice. The pot was filled with fried rice. Since then they did not do any labour and ate rice without doing any work. His wife used to wash the rice utensils in the river. The villagers asked

the man, and he narrated the whole story to them. The villagers wanted to visit heaven. The man agreed to take them to heaven. Everyone cleaned their cloths, smeared oil on their heads. At night, when the elephant came, the man caught the elephant's leg. Others grabbed the legs one after another and made a chain. The elephant flew to the sky. In the middle of the sky, the villagers asked the first man, how much food do they give? The man said, "Too much." Villagers asked, "Do they give a full meal to fill the belly?" The man said, "Yes." The villagers asked, "How many times will the gods feed us in a day?" The man was irritated, angry and showed his two hands and said, "People of heaven give us food twice a day." No sooner did he say this than he forgot that he had left the elephant's tail. The elephant fled to the sky, and the villagers, with the man, fell on the earth. They became a heap of bones. The villagers thus ended their lives.

title: The Greedy Monkey
text_english: Once upon a time a monkey noticed some wheat which had fallen into a small hollow in a rock. Thrusting in his hand, he filled it with the grain, but the entrance was so narrow that he was unable to draw it out without relinquishing most of his prize. This, however, he was unwilling to do, greedily desiring to have it all. So the consequence was that he remained without any, and finally went hungry away.

title: The Jackal and the Flees
text_english:
There was once a jackal so infested with fleas that life was a burden to him. Determined to be rid of them, he sought for a pool of water, and snatching up a small piece of dry wood in his mouth, he began to enter the water with "measured steps and slow." Gradually, as he advanced, the astonished fleas rushed up his legs and took refuge on his back. The rising water again drove them in multitudes from his back to his head, and from his head to his nose, whence they escaped on to the piece of wood, which became perfectly black with them.

When the sly jackal perceived the situation of his foes, he suddenly bobbed his head into the water, relinquished the wood, and with a chuckle swam back to the shore, leaving the feas to their fate.

title: The Seven Wise Men of Buneyr
text_english:
Seven men of Buneyr once left their native wilds for the purpose of seeking their fortunes. When evening came they all sat down under a tree to rest, when one of them said, "Let us count to see if we are all here." So he counted, "One, two, three, four, five, six," but, quite omitting to reckon himself, he exclaimed, "There's one of us missing, we are only six!"

"Nonsense!" cried the others, and the whole company of seven began counting with uplifted forefingers, but they all forgot to count themselves.

Fearing some evil, they now rose up, and at once set out to search for their missing comrade. Presently they met a shepherd, who greeted them civilly and said, "Friends, why are you in such low spirits?"

"We have lost one of our party," answered they; "we started this morning seven in number, and now we are only six. Have you seen any one of us hereabouts?"

"But," said the shepherd, "seven you are, for I have found your lost companion; behold: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven!"

"Ah," answered the wise men of Buneyr, "you have indeed found our missing brother. We owe you a debt of gratitude. Because you have done us this service, we insist on doing a month's free labor for you."

So the shepherd, overjoyed with his good fortune, took the men home with him.

Now, the shepherd's mother was a very old woman, in her dotage, utterly feeble and unable to help herself. When the morning came he placed her under the care of one of the Buneyris, saying to him, "You will stay here and take care of my old mother."

To another Buneyri he said, "You take out my goats, graze them on the hills by day, and watch over them by night."

To the other five he said, "As for you, I shall have work for you tomorrow."

The man who was left in charge of the old crippled mother found that his time was fully occupied in the constant endeavor to drive off the innumerable flies which in that hot season kept her in a state of continual excitement and irritation. When, however, he saw that all his efforts were fruitless, and that he flapped the wretches away in vain, he became desperate, and, lifting up a large stone, he aimed it deliberately at a certain fly which had settled on the woman's face. Hurling it with all his might, he of course missed the fly, but, alas! he knocked the woman prone on her back. When the shepherd saw this he wrung his hands in despair. "Ah," cried he, "what has your stupidity done for me? The fly has escaped, but as for my poor old mother, you have killed her dead."

Meanwhile, the second Buneyri led his flock of goats up and down among the hills, and when midday came he rested to eat his bread, while many of the assembled goats lay down beside him. As he was eating he began to observe how the goats were chewing the cud and occasionally looking at him So he foolishly imagined that they were mocking him, and waxed wroth. "So," cried he, "because I am taking my food, you must needs crowd round and make game of me, must you?" And, seizing his hatchet, he made a sudden rush at the poor animals, and he had already struck off the heads of several of them, when the shepherd came running to the spot, bemoaning his bad luck and crying to the fellow to desist from slaughter.

That night was a sorrowful one for the trustful shepherd, and bitterly he repented his rashness. In the morning the remaining five wise men of Buneyr came to him, and said, "It is now our turn. Give us some work to do, too!"

"No, no, my friends," answered he; "you have amply repaid me for the trifling favor I did for you in finding your missing companion; and now, for God's sake, go your way and let me see you no more."

Hearing these words, the wise men of Buneyr resumed their journey.

title: The Farmer, the Crocodile, and the Jackal
text_english:
There was once a wily old crocodile who dwelt in a tank [pond] hard by a village, and he was sometimes so ferocious that he would seize children who used to go for water there, then drown and eat them. He had become, in fact, the terror of the place.

One year there was a very great drought, and the tank by degrees began to dry up, and at last it got quite dry, and the crocodile was to be seen grilling and roasting in the sun.

He used to call out to the passers-by, "Oh! pray take pity upon me and show me where I can go for water, for I am dying in this heat."

"No, indeed! they all said. "We are glad to see you suffering, for have you not often made us suffer by taking our goats, and sometimes even our children? We shall not help you in any way."

At last an old man passed by, and the crocodile appealed to him, and at first he replied as the others did, but afterwards he relented and said, "Well, if you will follow me I will take you to a tank which is never dry." So the crocodile followed him, and he showed him a tank no great distance off, which was filled with water.

The old man went first into the tank himself, and calling to the crocodile, he said, "See here, how deep it is!"

No sooner had the crocodile had a good drink, than he made a grab at the old man's leg. "Ah-ho! Ah-ho!" said the old man. "What are you doing?"

"Well," replied the crocodile, "I have had a good drink, thanks to you, and as I have had no food for many days, I am going to make a meal of you. That is what I am going to do."

"You wretched and ungrateful brute!" said the old man. "Is this the way you reward me?"

At that moment a jackal hove in sight, coming for a drink (the jackals, we know, are the most cunning of all animals), and the old man said, "I will put my case before him, and if he says you are to eat me, very good, so you shall."

The old man then beckoned to the jackal to come close up to the tank, and told him all the facts of the case.

The jackal said, "You know I am always a just judge, and if you want me to decide, you must show me the place from whence you brought the crocodile."

So they all three wended their way back to the tank near the village, and the jackal said, "Show me the exact spot where you first found the crocodile," and when they got there the jackal said, "Now I am going to give you my judgment, so prepare to listen." Then turning to the old man, he said quietly, "You silly old idiot! What made you ever help a crocodile? Now, you run one way, and I will run the other."

The jackal gave a skip, and was soon off out of sight, and the old man took to his heels also, and soon got away. The wily old crocodile, now balked of his prey, said to himself, "I know my way back to that water tank, and I will someday have my revenge on that jackal, for he is sure to come there to lap water."

So back he went, and as there were many trees near the tank, some of whose roots went beneath the water, the crocodile lay in ambush there. By and by the jackal came to drink water, and the crocodile made a sudden snap at his leg, and held it.

"Oh, you foolish crocodile!" the jackal said, "you think you have got hold of my leg, do you? But it is only the root of a tree."

Hearing this, the crocodile released his hold, and the jackal jumped off in high glee out of his reach.

The crocodile then determined that he would try some other plan of entrapping him. So, as there were great numbers of a small fruit falling from one of the trees, which he knew the jackal came to eat, he one night piled up a heap and hid himself beneath it, leaving only his eyes uncovered.

Presently the jackal came prowling along, and noticing the pile of fruit he felt inclined to partake of some, but he drew near very cautiously, and in a moment he caught sight of the two eyes of the crocodile glistening in the moonlight, when he called out, "Oh, I see you!" and scampered off.

After this, the crocodile saw that it was no use to try himself to catch the jackal, "for," said he, "he is too cunning for me. I must employ someone who comes to get water here."

So one day he saw a farmer, and said to him, "If you will catch a jackal for me, I will make you a rich man, for I will give you several jewels which people have dropped in this tank for years and years, and they are lying here at the bottom."

"Oh!" replied the farmer, "that is easily done." So that very night he went into the jungle and lay down as if dead.

Presently the jackal made his appearance, and smelling along he came close up to the body. Then he hesitated and said, "I wonder if this is really a dead body or not." He then called out audibly, "If it is really dead it will shake its leg, and if it is alive it won't do so." This he said so quickly and so artfully that the farmer was taken aback, and to make him believe he was dead he at once stupidly shook his leg, and off skipped the jackal, saying, "I caught you there," and was lost to view in an instant.

The farmer, who was very avaricious, and wanted the jewels badly, made up his mind that he would by hook or by crook make sure of the jackal on the next occasion. So this time he prepared of the softest wax a doll the size of a child, and digging a small grave and covering it over with leaves and mud, he waited in hiding to see the result.

Shortly after sunset the jackal began to prowl about as usual, and coming on the new grave he said to himself, "Ah! This is someone lately buried. I will try my luck here." He then began to scratch with his paw, and presently one paw got caught in the wax, and in trying to get that away, all four became stuck with the wax, when in a moment out came the farmer from his hiding place and said, "Ah! At last I have got you, and you are my prisoner!"

The jackal yelled and howled, and endeavored to escape, but was hindered by the wax on his feet. So then he took to frightening the farmer, and said, "If you do not get me out of this scrape I will call all the jackals in a moment of time, and they will destroy you forever, for do you not know that I am the king of the jackals?"

"What am I to do?" asked the farmer.

"Go!" he said. "Go and get some oil, and rub it all over me. Then get a fowl, and tie it about fifty yards away, and bring two men with hatchets to stand over me, so that if I attempt to get away they may chop me to pieces!"

This being done by the farmer, the jackal while being held in his hands sought his opportunity, and being well greased all over, he made a violent spring and so got clear of the farmer. Then he dashed between the legs of the men with hatchets, when they made a plunge at him, but they only succeeded in hurting their own legs. So the jackal got finally off, and picking up the fowl, he was soon lost to view, and so won the day.

title: Shazi and the Flying Paratha
text_english:
One morning Shazi had sat down to eat breakfast when Ammi [mother] baked a big round paratha [layered flatbread]. As soon as Ammi turned to look for the butter, the fan became fast. The paratha went "flutter flutter" and flew up into the air, like a paper moon. Shazi cried out, "Ammi! Our breakfast has become a pilot!"

The paratha first landed on the wardrobe, then wrapped itself around the curtain. The cat leapt, but fell down with flour on its face. Nani [maternal grandmother] laughed and said, "This is not a paratha; it is a mischievous airplane!" Shazi took hold of a chair and began going around after it.

When Shazi tapped the plate with a spoon, "thak thak," the paratha slowly began to come down. But after coming down, it landed straight on the head of the dog Topo. Topo suddenly looked as if he were wearing a paratha hat. Everyone in the house laughed so much that even the tea spilled.

At last Ammi picked up the paratha, made pieces of it, and shared them with everyone. Shazi said, "Now it cannot fly, but it can certainly go into the stomach!" Topo too began looking for his paratha hat, and everyone laughed again. After that, at every breakfast Shazi would say, "First turn off the fan, then present the paratha!"

A laughter-filled breakfast story of Shazi, Topo, and a paratha [layered flatbread] flying through the air.

title: Rano and the Talking Parrot
text_english:
Rano was a dear little girl who sang songs every day in the courtyard. One morning a green parrot came and sat on the wall and said, "Rano, come with me!" Rano laughed and said, "Oh! This parrot really does talk!" Slowly, slowly, she set off behind the parrot toward the garden.

In the garden there was a tiny door, covered with flowering vines. The parrot said, "Open the door; here is the secret of laughter!" When Rano opened the door, colorful butterflies began flying inside. Rano clapped with joy and said, "Wow! This is a magical garden!"

Suddenly a fat frog climbed with a splash onto a leaf and slipped and fell down. Rano laughed so much that the parrot beside her also began going "hahaha." The frog said shyly, "I can dance too; look!" Then he started dancing with little hops.

Rano, the parrot, and the frog kept playing and laughing all through the garden. The butterflies kept circling round and round above them, as though a fair had begun. When she returned home, Rano said, "Today my greatest treasure was laughter!" After that, every morning she would say, "Laugh, play, and share happiness!"

Rano, a lovely laughter-filled story about a talking parrot and a magical garden.

title: Today Even the Pillow Sneezed!
text_english:
At noon Ayesha was sitting in her room with a storybook. Suddenly a sound came from her bed: "achoo... achoo!" Ayesha said in fright, "Oh Lord, has the pillow caught a cold?" Slowly, slowly, she moved forward and began looking toward the pillow.

As soon as she lifted the pillow, a little Billo [cat] came out from underneath. There was flour on the cat's face, and black pepper grains were on its nose. Billo sneezed again, "achoo!" and went straight into the clothes basket. Ayesha laughed so much that the book in her hand turned upside down.

Ammi [mother] came running and said, "Is this a room, or a fair of sneezes?" Just then Billo came out of the basket and clung to the curtain. When the curtain moved, Dadi [paternal grandmother] said, "It seems there is no ghost in the house; it is a peppery cat!" Now the whole household was doubled over with laughter.

At last Ayesha cleaned Billo's face and gave it milk. Billo sat down comfortably, but every now and then gave another soft little "achoo." Ayesha said, "Today my pillow turned out to be more entertaining than my book!" After that, whenever the room was quiet, everyone would laugh and ask, "The pillow is all right, isn't it?"

A laughter-filled mischief story of Ayesha, Billo sneezing from pepper, and what came out from under the pillow.

title: Chann and the Flying Balloon
text_english:
Channu was a little cheerful boy who became happy over every little thing. From a fair he had got a yellow balloon, which shone very beautifully. Channu said to the balloon, "You are my friend; do not go far away!" But a gust of wind came, and the balloon flew away.

Channu ran after it, "Stop, stop, my yellow balloon!" The balloon went into the garden, where it got caught on a branch. A myna bird was sitting there, and she said, "I will help; do not be afraid!" Channu laughed and said, "Well done, myna; you are very wise!"

The myna shook the branch with her beak, but the balloon climbed even higher. Just then a monkey came, leapt up, and climbed the tree. The monkey gently brought the balloon down and placed it in Channu's hand. Channu said happily, "Wow! Today I have found true friends in the garden!"

Channu shared sweet biscuits with the myna and the monkey, and everyone began to dance. The yellow balloon kept swaying in the air, as though it too were celebrating happiness. Channu said, "I found the balloon, but friends are even dearer than that!" After that, every day he would say, "Share happiness, and increase your friends!"

A lovely story of friendship and help in the search for Channu's yellow balloon.

title: Pappu and the Hat-Wearing Goat
text_english:
Pappu was sitting in the courtyard eating roti [flatbread] when his goat Leelo came running in. Leelo took Nani's [maternal grandmother's] large hat in her mouth and pulled it up onto her head. The hat tilted to one side, and the goat's ears came out. Pappu laughed so much that even the roti in his hand turned upside down.

Wearing the hat, Leelo bleated "maa maa" as if she were a school mistress. Pappu said, "Very well then, now recite the lesson!" The goat climbed straight onto the stool, but the hat came down over her eyes. Going forward and forward, she ended up putting her face into a bucket.

The bucket got stuck on her head, and instead of "maa maa," Leelo began making "boon boon" sounds. Pappu laughed until he was doubled over and said, "Oh, this is not a goat; it is a brass band!" Hearing the noise, the hen, the cat, and the duck also came near. Seeing it, the duck flapped her wings as if saying, "What spectacle is this?"

Nani came, gently opened the bucket, and took the hat off Leelo's head too. Leelo, embarrassed, hid behind Pappu, but kept wagging her tail. Pappu said, "Nani, the funniest goat of all lives in our house!" And from that day on, everyone began calling Leelo "the schoolmistress goat."

A mischievous story full of laughter, about Pappu and Leelo's hat and bucket.

title: When the Shoe Ran Away
text_english:
Early in the morning Hana was getting ready for school. She had put on one shoe, but the other shoe could not be found anywhere. Suddenly, from beneath the charpai [woven cot], came the sound "thap thap." Hana bent down and looked, and the shoe was sliding forward all by itself!

Hana said, "Hey, stop! Are you going to school, or are you off to win a running race?" The shoe slipped across the floor and entered the kitchen. There the cat leapt at it, thinking it was a mouse, but fell into the basket itself. Ammi [mother] laughed so much that the spoon in her hand also fell down.

The shoe then went into the courtyard and stopped beside the tub of water. The duck pecked into it and then tried to sit on top of it. Hana said, "Wow! Now my shoe has become a boat too!" The duck slipped down and, saying "quack quack," began going round and round.

At last Dadi [paternal grandmother] picked up the shoe and looked inside it; a tiny toy fan was stuck in it. The fan kept running, and that was why the shoe had been running around. Hana, Ammi, Dadi, and the duck all laughed so much that the courtyard echoed. After that, every day before putting on her shoe, Hana would say, "First I will ask: today will you walk, or will you run?"

A mischievous, laughter-filled story of Hana's runaway shoe, the cat, and the duck.

title: Guddu and the Upside-Down Umbrella
text_english:
Guddu was a little mischievous boy who loved splashing in the rain very much. One day he picked up Nani's [maternal grandmother's] big umbrella and went out into the courtyard. But in his hurry he held the umbrella upside down. Instead of falling down, all the water began gathering above his head!

Guddu said, "Wow! My umbrella is a bucket too!" He was walking along laughing when a duck came near. The duck saw water in the upside-down umbrella and immediately splashed inside it. Now there was an umbrella on Guddu's head, and in the umbrella a duck was swimming!

Guddu ran home and said, "Nani! Look, I have made a walking pond!" Nani laughed so much that her spectacles became crooked. Just then the cat came too and began staring in amazement at the umbrella. The duck said "quack quack," and the cat, frightened, climbed onto the stool.

When Nani turned the umbrella the right way, all the water splashed down onto Guddu. Guddu, the duck, and Nani were all doubled over with laughter. Guddu said, "Today I learned that an umbrella saves the head; it does not bathe ducks!" After that, whenever it rained, everyone would laugh and call him "Guddu of the pond."

A delightful story of Guddu, the duck, and the funny pond made inside an upside-down umbrella.

title: The Day the Wardrobe Laughed
text_english:
Nimra was a little mischievous girl who was always looking for something new. One morning she opened the wardrobe to take out clothes, and from inside came the sound "hee hee hee." Nimra stepped back in fear and said, "Ammi [mother]! Our clothes have started laughing!"

Ammi came and opened the wardrobe again, but now everything was quiet. As soon as Ammi turned away, the sound "hahaha" came from inside again. Nimra peeped inside slowly, and the pile of her socks was moving.

Suddenly a little monkey came out from among the socks, with Abba's [father's] cap on its head. Holding a handkerchief in one hand and making faces as if it had become a teacher, it was laughing. Nimra laughed so much that she sat down on the floor and began to say, "This is not a wardrobe; it is a circus!"

The monkey jumped up onto the clothesline and made a sock into a microphone. It kept going "oo oo aa aa," and Nani [maternal grandmother] also doubled over with laughter. At last it was given a banana, and it happily leapt out through the window.

Nimra said, "Today I learned that even in a pile of socks, a secret may be hidden!" After that, whenever the wardrobe opened, everyone would first laugh and ask, "There is no monkey inside, is there?" And Nimra would say softly, "Even if there is, let me laugh first!"

A laughter-filled, delightful story of Nimra, the wardrobe, the socks, and a mischievous monkey.

title: Round, Long, and a Small Star
text_english:
There was a little girl named Aina. Aina loved her toys very much. One day she was sitting in the courtyard looking at her toys when Ammi [mother] said, "Today we will learn new things while playing."

Ammi picked up a ball and asked, "What kind of shape is this?" Aina laughed and said, "It is round!" Ammi said, "Well done! A ball is round." Then she picked up a pencil. Aina said, "It is long!" Ammi happily said, "Exactly, a pencil is long."

Then Ammi placed a tiny bead in her hand. "What kind of thing is this?" Aina looked carefully and said, "It is small!" Ammi said, "Yes, a small bead." Then she showed her a big pillow. Aina clapped and said, "This is big!"

At breakfast time Ammi said, "Now tell me the colors too." She showed an apple. Aina said, "Red!" She showed a banana. "Yellow!" She showed a leaf. "Green!" Ammi said, "Wow! My dear girl has learned so much!"

In the evening Aina herself chose and arranged her toys. The round ball on one side, the long pencil on another side, the small beads in a little plate, and the big pillow on the charpai [woven cot]. She laughed and said, "Ammi, now I know round, long, small, big, and colors too!"

Ammi hugged Aina and said, "When children learn with love, everything looks beautiful to them." Aina looked toward the sky. A small star was shining there. She said softly, "Now I will learn something new every day!" The story ended, and the learning remained.

A sweet educational story in which Aina learns shapes, sizes, and colors while playing with her mother.

title: What Was in the Cloud's Pocket?
text_english:
There was a little girl named Maheen. Maheen loved looking at the sky very much. Every day she would think, "Clouds are so light, but what is inside them?" One day she was sitting on the roof when a small, round, chubby cloud bent down. The cloud spoke softly, "Maheen, you look toward me every day. What is the matter?" Maheen, surprised, said, "I wonder what is in your pocket."

The cloud laughed. It shook its soft edges and said, "Come, have a look." As soon as Maheen came near, strange and wondrous things began coming out of the cloud's pocket. On one side were tiny little pieces of laughter, shining brightly. On another side lay young women's lullabies, birds' songs, and children's unfinished questions. In one corner, raindrops were sitting in a row. Maheen said, "Wow! This is a treasure!" The cloud said, "Not every cloud has only water; some clouds also keep memories safe."

Just then a soft gust of wind came, and a little bottle of golden drops fell from the cloud's pocket. Maheen caught it at once. "What is this?" she asked. The cloud, a little shy, said, "This is a special drop. Wherever it falls, laughter grows there. But it must be used carefully." Maheen kept the bottle safe. Down in the lane, a little boy was sitting sadly because his clay toys had broken. Maheen let one drop from the bottle fall near him. As soon as the drop touched the ground, the clay began to shine gently, and the broken toys became even more beautiful. The boy laughed.

Then Maheen sprinkled one drop in the quiet courtyard of the school. The fragrance of flowers came there. She dropped one drop near Nani [maternal grandmother], and Nani remembered an old lullaby. A sweet voice rang through the whole house. By evening, the bottle had become empty. Maheen looked upward. The cloud was now climbing back toward the sky. Maheen called out, "Now, if I need more drops?" The cloud smiled and said, "Wherever you yourself give happiness to someone, there a new cloud comes into being."

After that, Maheen understood that the real magic was not in the bottle. The real magic was in her own heart. Wherever she went, she went about sharing love, laughter, and happiness. The story ended, and the sign of happiness remained.

A gentle, lovely story of Maheen, the cloud's pocket, and magical drops of happiness.

title: The Bridge of Colors
text_english:
There was a beautiful garden, which always remained filled on every side with colorful flowers. People called it "the Garden of Colors." There lived a little six-year-old girl named Mahi. Every morning Mahi played in the garden with her little friends, and a playful little Phuli was her greatest friend. One day Phuli came in alarm and began to say, "Mahi! The rainbow of the sky is disappearing. If the colors are not brought back, the colors of the flowers will also grow pale!" Mahi immediately picked up her little bag, asked Ammi [mother] for permission, and said with a smile, "Do not worry; we will bring the colors back."

Mahi and Phuli first went toward the fields. The wheat was waving golden. Mahi raised both hands in the air and said, "This is our yellow color!" Then they reached the bank of the canal. The water looked like blue glass. Mahi put blue pebbles into the bag. "We have found the blue color too!" Farther on, under the great banyan tree, there was cool shade. The green leaves rustled in the wind, and Mahi felt as if they were saying, "Take it with love; our green color is yours too!" Now there were three colors in the bag, but the rainbow needed more colors.

The orange color would be with the setting sun! They all climbed onto the mound. The sun went down and the sky became orange. Phuli caught a shining ray with her wing and placed it in the bag. At night they went into the flower garden. Red roses were fragrant there. Mahi gently touched a rose, and its red color was obtained too. Now only one color was left: purple.
