The puri began repeating the same boast: "I have come out of the kadhai, escaped from Buddhu's mother, defeated five young men, made a fool of Tail-Cut Rabbit, and tricked Ear-Cut Fox. Now, Lady Dog‚ " It had only said this much when the bitch snapped at it with a quick bite, and half the puri went into her mouth. The half-puri that remained ran away with such speed that, a little farther on, no one knows how, it slipped into the earth. The bitch and her pups searched and searched for the puri until they were tired out, but no trace of it could be found. That bitch and her pups spent their whole lives looking for that puri, but what was not to be found was not found. To this day, all dogs go about sniffing the ground in search of that half-puri, hoping that if they catch its scent somewhere, they will dig it out. It had vanished into the earth.

title: Fireflies of Fire
text_english: Winter was at its height, and in those days Suraj Baba [Father Sun] was staying on a high mountain. In a valley near Chitral there was a village where an old woman named Amina was cooking in her house. Suddenly a spark flew from the stove and fell on a cloth. She paid no attention. The spark became a flame, and only when it began taking hold of the things around it did the old woman come to her senses. She tried very hard to put out the fire, but it kept spreading, and before anyone could do anything the hut burned to ashes. The old woman was deeply distressed, for she had no money with which to build another hut. Out of helplessness she went to live with one of her relatives. As the days passed, her grief and anger kept growing. She began to speak ill of fire. She would say, "This fire is terribly cruel. If I had the power, I would destroy it." One day, when she learned that Suraj Baba had taken up his place on the mountain, she filled a sack with the ashes of her hut and began climbing the mountain to complain to Suraj Baba about Fire. After walking the whole day, she reached the mountain top. There she saw a great ball of light. There was a very old man whose face shone brightly. The old woman greeted him, sat down on the sack, and said, panting, "Suraj Baba! I have come to you on urgent business. Fire has burned down my home. You must punish it." Suraj Baba heard her complaint and summoned Fire. Soon Fire arrived. She too appeared in the form of a woman. Old Amina cried out angrily, "Yes, this is the one who ruined me!" Fire was astonished to hear this, then said, "It was not my fault. You were careless, and that day the wind was strong as well." Suraj Baba looked toward Amina questioningly. Embarrassed, she said, "Yes, perhaps that is what happened that day, but Fire is very cruel. It often becomes a calamity for human beings." "I am also a mercy for human beings, and a means by which life remains connected and sustained," Fire said quickly. "No. You have always harmed us," the old woman said in anger. "Very well. If you want to see my worth, come with me," said Fire, also angered. The old woman looked at her in surprise. Fire spoke again: "Take my hand and close your eyes. We shall return in a little while." Fearfully, the old woman took Fire's hand. Fire murmured something under her breath, and the two of them disappeared from that place. "Now open your eyes," Fire's voice said after a while. When the old woman opened her eyes she was amazed. They were standing in a cold region where a snowstorm was raging. All the trees and fields were covered with a sheet of snow, yet the old woman did not feel cold. Fire said softly, "As long as you hold my hand, you will not feel the cold." Then they went forward. A short distance away they saw the mouth of a cave. Both of them entered. Inside they saw two farmers. They had been returning home after their work when the storm overtook them, and to save themselves from the cold they had taken refuge in the cave. The bitter cold had left them in a wretched state. One farmer lay curled up like a bundle, as if he had lost consciousness. The other still had his senses, though his teeth were chattering too. He had gathered some dry grass and pieces of wood and was trying to light a fire by striking two stones together. The two women stood silently watching them. The men could not see them. At last sparks flew from the stones and fell on the grass. The man quickly began blowing on them. First the dry grass caught fire, then the wood also began to burn. The cave suddenly filled with light. The man called to his companion and brought him close to the fire. Soon the heat of the flames restored the other man's senses, and he began to feel comfort in the warmth. Outside, the storm was fierce and flakes of snow were flying everywhere, but the cave was warm, and those inside sat in ease. Fire looked at the old woman questioningly. The old woman nodded in agreement. Then the two of them came out. A little later they were again before Suraj Baba. Fire said, "You saw how, by God's command, I helped those afflicted people. Otherwise, perhaps they would have lost their lives." "Yes, I understand," the old woman said. "God has made everything for human benefit. Harm comes from our own carelessness." Then she thanked Suraj Baba and Fire and started back toward the village. Fire was with her. As they descended the mountain slope, Fire asked the old woman, "Why are you carrying that sack?" At this the old woman suddenly started. "Oh! I had completely forgotten it. Well, what use is it to me now?" Saying this, she threw the sack there. "What was in it?" Fire asked in surprise. "The ashes of my hut," the old woman said sadly. After they had walked a little farther, Fire said Khuda Hafiz [farewell] and disappeared behind a hill. The old woman went on toward her village. When she reached the outskirts, she saw her sack lying beneath a tree. She was greatly astonished. The sack felt heavy. "Why, how did this come here?" she wondered. Then she opened the mouth of the sack, and her eyes opened wide. The sack was full of gold ashrafis [gold coins]. Happily the old woman took it with her. Then she had a house built for herself and bought an animal farm for her livelihood. The ashrafis that remained she distributed among the villagers. They too had their houses rebuilt properly. Everyone began to live happily. Yet the old woman often wondered where those ashrafis had come from. One day she was cooking food for her son. The fire was burning brightly. It seemed as though tiny gold coins were glittering along the wall of the stove. She began looking carefully at the fire. The little flickering fireflies of flame looked very lovely. She felt that Fire was saying something to her. She kept looking, and then suddenly she understood. Smiling, she said, "I understand. It was you who helped me by God's command. Truly, you too are a mercy for us." She felt that the tiny leaping flames had smiled all at once on hearing her words. They say that even today, when the fireflies of flame sparkle along the walls of the stove, they remind people of that old woman.

title: Mas Janali [Moonlit Playing Field]
text_english: Momo [maternal uncle]...! Momo...! " Abdullah Yugui wiped the sweat on his forehead and looked in the direction of the voice. His nephew was coming towards him saying Momo [maternal uncle], Momo [maternal uncle] in Balti language. God bless you. " He thought in his heart, then put the "hoe" on his shoulder and held the "shovel" in his hand and put it on the ground. (What happened?) Abdullah Yugovi asked worriedly as he approached his nephew. His nephew tried to speak but was unable to due to heavy breathing. He panted and pointed to one side. When Abdullah looked, it seemed as if there was a crowd of people somewhere in the distance. On reflection, he felt as if they were all coming towards him. He wasn't wrong, the crowd was moving towards him. Soon the scene started to become clear and the faces of the people started to be seen. Abdullah muttered. Niyat Qubal Hayat was the ruler of Ghizer district. He was accompanied by many local youths who, like Abdullah himself, carried shovels and shovels. After a while, all the questions in his heart were answered. On the instructions of his ruler, he along with other youths started the work of paving a large field. Abdullah Yugwi hit the hoe on the ground and sat down on a pile of dirt. He was at a height of twelve and a half thousand feet above the sea level, but still the sweat was flowing like water. This was the case not only with him but all his companions were drenched in sweat. He took a deep breath and went back to work. Hours turned into days and days into weeks. His sovereign intention, Qubal Hayat was constantly busy encouraging him. Finally, the time came when the piece of land, about 56 meters wide and 200 meters long, was completely leveled. It was not an easy task, but human courage and courage made it easy. Niyat Qubal Hayat was informed that the work was completed, and then he rushed there. He took one look at the field and imagined the face of the British political agent "Evelyn Hey Cobb" beaming with joy at the sight of the field. A few days later, when all the preparations were completed, "EH Cobb" visited the field. The work was more magnificent than he expected. He offered a very high reward to Niyat Qubal Hayat. When are such works completed in the lure of rewards? Neet Qubal Hayat was thinking about his forefathers, especially Ali Sher Khan Inchan, who conquered this entire area and made "Mas Janali" here for the first time and started a game like "Chogan [polo]". While thinking, it occurred to him that he made a strange request to E. H. Cobb. "Just get it done, I'll take it as my reward. " E. H. Cobb hesitated for a moment and then said: "All right. It will be as you wish. " Shanza also quickly saddled his Arabian horse. The horse neighed and then galloped at the rider's command. This horse belonged to his uncle. When Shanza saw her red and white Lala running this gray horse, she would start reciting Mashallah, Mashallah. He did not understand whether Lala was glorifying the horse or the horse belonged to Lala. Lala knew that Shanza was very fond of horse riding. He himself made him an excellent horseman. Even at that time, Shanza was running with a long polo stick in her hand. She always wanted to get "the ball" but it was not happening. The players of the other team were constantly throwing mallets at each other. Before they could score, one of Shanza's teammates grabbed the ball. In the next moment puranjo was moving towards Shanza. Shanza skilfully intercepted her and pushed her forward. She was currently in the historical field of "Mas Janali". "Chogan [polo]" was at its peak and they were up against a highly skilled team from Chitral. Shanza was part of the Baltistan team and at that time she was riding her horse Lala. Shanza was startled at the thought that he was part of the team instead of Lala. Time suddenly stopped and he felt the field of Shandur begin to float with rising clouds. Instead of running, the horses started to fly and even the padanjo got wings. She was moving ahead leaving behind all the players of the opposing team. Approaching the goal, he raised the hockey in the air and that was the moment when his balance b It collapsed. With a low cry, Shanza got down from the horse. The ground was not there, she felt that she was falling down. How was this sound? Lala's voice from the next room hit Shanza's ears. She, who herself was looking around in surprise, suddenly came to her senses. He remembered the dream he had a few moments ago. "Shanza? " When Lala's voice was heard again, she immediately said: "Nothing, Lala! My shirt fell down. " "The sound of the shirt falling was not much? " Lala knocked on the door and entered smiling, "Yes Lala! It was inside the shirt too. " Shanza said as he got up from the ground. Laughing, Lala patted him and said with a smile: "Thankfully, you play polo in your dreams, otherwise you would have been injured many times. " "There is no such thing now. " Shanza said feeling embarrassed, Lala laughed again, "By the way, Lala! Have girls ever played this game in history? " Shanza asked innocently, "Bhai! I don't think so, but you still want to ask Baba about this. " "Baba? " Shanza hesitated. It was too late for Lala to say, Shanza immediately got up and wrapped her hair and walked towards Baba's room......*.... "What did she want, Baba? " Shanza was still confused about the reward of Niyat Qubal Hayat, which was given to all the people of Gilgit and Baltistan for making Mass Janali. Shanza got up and in no time the steamed trout fish was in front of Baba. Shanza spoke in an annoyed tone. He just wanted an answer to his question. "Which rivers meet at such a height? Then how can a river from another country meet Pakistani rivers? Yes, it is possible that this fish was ordered from another country and put into the lakes here. " "From another country...? But it lives in cold water and which countries have more cold water? " Shanza fell into thinking, "Hey, hey! Is this not the result of the reward that Niyat Qabool Hayat asked for? " He was suddenly shocked and Baba smiled and nodded yes. Shanza also told his friends with amusement how polo, or chogan started and how the local ruler asked a British officer for a trout fish as a reward. His request was fulfilled. Today, due to this ruler of Shandur district of Baltistan, not only polo is played all over the country, but trout fish is also eaten with great enthusiasm.

title: Mehrunnisa and the Green Fairy
text_english: What was the secret that she was changing day by day? Many centuries ago, in the green valley of Kashmir, a little girl lived with her father and her stepmother. Her name was Mehrunnisa. Her stepmother was jealous and cruel. Her father was a farmer and worked in the fields all day; he too was afraid of the stepmother's sharp tongue. The stepmother made Mehrunnisa do all the household chores and gave her the previous night's leftovers to eat. Sometimes Mehrunnisa even had to go hungry. The rule of the house was in the hands of the stepmother. All day long Mehrunnisa kept silently busy with work. One day, while grazing the goats, Mehrunnisa wandered a little way beyond her own area. On the bank of the Neelum River there was a dense forest. As she was passing through it, she suddenly heard a woman's voice. "Listen, good girl! Can you help me?" Startled, Mehrunnisa followed the voice and saw, a short distance away among the bushes, a beautiful fairy with green eyes. One of her wings had been caught in the thorns, and despite all her efforts she could not free it. Pain showed on her face. Mehrunnisa was astonished to see the lovely fairy in such a condition. She was a very compassionate and virtuous girl. She came near the fairy and asked, "Who are you?" The fairy raised her shining green eyes and looked at her. There were tears in them. "I have come from Paristan [the land of fairies]. My name is the Green Fairy. As I was passing this way, one of my wings became caught in the thorns. Can you free my wing from them?" Hearing this, Mehrunnisa stepped carefully through the thorns and came close to the Green Fairy. Then she gently released the fairy's wing. The Green Fairy felt some relief, though she was still slightly wounded. Mehrunnisa seated her by the riverbank and ran home. A hundred thanks that her stepmother was not in the house; she had gone to visit a relative. Mehrunnisa took ointment and lukewarm water and returned to the fairy. She washed the Green Fairy's wound with the warm water and applied the ointment. The fairy now began to feel better. She could fly back to Paristan. She was extremely pleased with Mehrunnisa. She said to her, "You are a good and noble girl. You helped me. Tell me, what do you want?" "I want food," Mehrunnisa answered in a low voice. On hearing this, the fairy stood still for a few moments. In her heart she felt the sorrow of innocent Mehrunnisa. Then, after a little silence, she took the pink flower from her hair and placed it in the girl's hand. "This flower is my gift to you. When you place it on vegetables, they will be cooked and set before you, and you will be able to eat your fill. When you place it on wheat or grain, cooked bread will come for you. When you place it on fruit, fruit sherbet will be prepared, and you will be able to drink as much as you like." Mehrunnisa looked closely at the flower. The magic flower was exceedingly beautiful. When she went out to graze the goats, she would, on her way back, pick grain, vegetables, and fruit from the forest and fields, hide them in her chador [shawl], and bring them home. At night, when everyone had gone to sleep, she would follow the fairy's instructions, eat delicious food, and then go to sleep. Her health and beauty began to bloom day by day. The stepmother wondered: "She eats only everyone's leftovers, and sometimes she even has to sleep hungry, yet she grows more beautiful every day. What is the secret?" She tried hard to discover it, but she did not succeed. Time passed, until Mehrunnisa turned eighteen. The fame of her beauty spread far and wide. One day the son of the village landlord rode into the forest to hunt. When he saw Mehrunnisa on the bank of the river, he remained staring at her. He had never seen such a beautiful girl before. He followed Mehrunnisa to her house, and the very next day his parents came to ask for her hand in marriage. Mehrunnisa's father was very happy that such a good proposal had come for his daughter, and he agreed at once. The stepmother burned with jealousy, but she had grown old now. Even though she wished to, she could not prevent Mehrunnisa's marriage. Mehrunnisa was married to the landlord's son with great celebration. The whole village rejoiced. The Green Fairy also attended the wedding. Mehrunnisa departed happily with her bridegroom.

title: Mangho Pir
text_english: My little friends! His real name is Khwaja Hassan Sakhi Sultan but he became known as Mangho Pir and the area is known by that name. Mangho Pir's dargah is on a hill in the northwest of Karachi. The ancestors of Khwaja Hasan Sakhi Sultan known as Mangho Pir came to the subcontinent in the 11th century. It is said that six to seven hundred years ago, the Sufi sage Baba Farid Ganj Shukar was going for Hajj with a convoy, that the then notorious bandit Manghwosa tried to rob the passengers, but being influenced by Baba Farid's good behavior, he accepted Islam and repented of his sins. After that, the same Manghu Wasa dedicated himself in the way of God. Local people say that the spring flowing near the court of Manghupir cures skin diseases, that is, if someone has skin problems, he should bathe in the water of the spring flowing near the Manghupir compound, he will be cured by God's command. According to experts, the water of this spring naturally contains sulfur, which is useful for curing skin diseases. Even today, pilgrims bathe with the water of this spring. Every year on the 8th of Dhu al-Hijjah, thousands of devotees celebrate the Urs of Sultan Sakhi Manghupir. A fair is held there before the month of Sawan called "Shadi Mela". Crocodiles are found here in the centuries-old pond. Sheedis are ancient residents of Karachi city. They have been devotees of this shrine for centuries. Their lifestyle is similar to that of Africans. Their ancestors had migrated from Africa years ago and settled here. They look like Africans in appearance. Animals are slaughtered and then the meat of these animals is fed to the crocodiles. On the occasion of Urs and Shidi Mela, the crocodiles in the pond are the center of public attention. Many interesting and amazing traditions are attributed to these crocodiles. The shrine is mentioned in 19th century writings. Remains of crocodiles are also found thousands of years old. According to many devotees, the crocodiles were born from the flowers that Mangho Pir Baba threw into the pond. According to some, they were lice and it is also said that Mangho Pir Baba used to ride on these crocodiles. Although there has never been any incident of crocodile attack here, the locals advise the devotees to be careful. According to experts, crocodiles are familiar with humans and depend on food given by pilgrims for sustenance and have lost the ability to hunt and eat on their own. Today, this hilly area in Karachi is known as Mangho Pir. The spring flowing near their premises has been watering its visitors for years.

title: Wisdom or Strength
text_english:
The Lion Once there was a lion. A fox also lived in that district. The lion was king of the animals. One day he fell ill, and the animals came to ask after him, saying, "How is His Majesty the king?" All the animals came, but the fox did not come. The lion asked the wolf, "Where is that fox?" The wolf said, "I do not know. Perhaps he has gone somewhere to eat and drink; he has no other business." The lion became very angry. He said, "If you had come, I would not have let them kill you." Some time later the fox appeared and came before the lion. The lion, who was very angry, said, "Why did you not come these past few days to ask after me? Everyone else came, but you did not come." The fox said, "Master, the rest of them only come and go uselessly. These few days I heard that you were unwell, so I went through the whole world in search of a physician. There is no physician before whom I did not go at least once. I said, 'Our lord the king is ill in such a way and suffers such pain; what is the cure for this?'" Brother, the lion was very pleased by this and asked, "Did you find any medicine?" The fox said, "The medicine is this: a donkey must be freshly slaughtered, and while the heart is still red and warm you must cut it out and eat it. You will be cured at once." The lion said, "Now where will you find a donkey?" The fox said, "Leave the donkey to me. I shall go and bring one easily."

So the fox went to look for a donkey, and the lion sat proudly waiting for his medicine. The fox wandered and wandered until he saw a fat, fine donkey grazing in a meadow. He went to him and said, "Come, let the two of us become friends." In short, the two became friends. They walked together, sat together, and talked together for a while, until they were good companions. Then the fox said, "Come, let us go to the other side of the mountain. There the water is so sweet and delightful, there are meadows and flowers and gardens. Come, enjoy yourself there. Why stay here? Let the two of us settle over there." The donkey said, "It will not do. Over there a wolf, or something like a wolf, or a lion may catch me." The fox said, "I am here; do not worry about that." He spoke and spoke until at last he brought the donkey near the mountain.

The lion was in a very bad state. When he rose from his place, he almost fainted at once. The fox brought the donkey close to the lion, left him near a rock, and went into the lion's cave whispering, "I have brought the donkey. Go; he is by the rock. Throw him down now!" The lion was delighted, rose up, roared, sprang upon the donkey, struck him with one blow, and knocked him over; then the lion himself fainted from the effort. At that moment the fox acted quickly: first he cut out the donkey's heart and ate it. After a little while the lion came back to his senses, got up, and said, "Wait, let me cut out the donkey's heart and eat it." He put his hand on the donkey and found the body still warm. "By God, how good!" he said. Brother, he intended to cut out and eat the heart, but when he searched there was no heart. He became angry at the fox and said, "Where is this donkey's heart?" The fox said, "Master, he had no heart." The lion said, "Have you ever seen a donkey without a heart?" The fox answered, "Master, he was so heartless that he came here. If he had had a heart, he would never have come."

In former times there was a fox who was very hungry and miserable. He wandered about looking for a morsel, saying, "Where shall I go to find food and be satisfied?" Wandering in this way, he entered a garden. He hoped that some hen or rooster or some such thing might fall into his hands. He searched and searched, and saw a piece of fat lying there. He went near, intending to eat it, but saw that it was set upon a trap; a farmer had fastened the fat to the trap so that some creature would come and be caught. Brother, however hard he tried, the fox could not eat it. He left the garden disappointed, thinking, "How can I eat this?" As he went along, a wolf happened to come by. The wolf said, "Where were you?" The fox said, "By God, I took a little turn in that garden. There is a very good piece of fat there. Go and eat it." The wolf said, "Why did you not eat it yourself?" The fox answered, "I was fasting. Today I could not eat." The wolf said, "Where is it? I will eat it." The fox said, "Come, I will show you. If I had not been fasting I would have eaten it myself." At last he led the wolf to the trap and said, "Here is the fat; take it and eat." The foolish wolf was hungry and leapt upon the fat, not noticing the trap. When he sprang, the trap caught him. The fox then jumped forward, seized the fat, and calmly ate it in front of him. The wolf said, "But were you not fasting a little while ago?" The fox answered, "Yes, but now I am breaking my fast." Then the farmer appeared, coming with a spade on his shoulder. The fox said, "Now recite your own iftar prayer, for your time to break fast has come."

There was also a king who was very cruel: he beat people, killed people, and lived in pleasure. This king had a very fine fat donkey. He used him, rode him everywhere, and worked him until finally the donkey grew old and his teeth fell out. When the donkey became old, the king said, "It is useless to give him fodder. Throw him into the wilderness. If I have him killed, that will bring sin." So they took him and threw him into the wild. There the poor animal grazed on whatever he could, drank what water he found, and lived as best he could. One day a wolf appeared and wanted to eat him. Several times he attacked the old donkey. The donkey begged, "Do not eat me. I am old; my meat will have no taste, and your teeth will not manage it." But the wolf would not agree. At last the donkey thought and said, "I am the king's donkey. Do not eat me. If you eat me and the king hears of it, he will kill all the wolves at once. This will not be good for you." The wolf said, "It cannot be helped; I must fill this hungry belly with your flesh."

At last the donkey said, "Come and look. If you do not believe that I am the king's donkey, my horseshoe is gold." The wolf said, "Where is it? Show me." The donkey raised his foot, and indeed the shoe shone like gold. The donkey said, "Since you are going to eat me, pull this shoe off with your teeth and take it to such-and-such mountain. There is a shepherd there with very fat lambs. Give him my golden shoe and he will give you two lambs. Eat those and go. When they are finished, come back and I will let you pull off another shoe; I have four." The wolf thought, "By God, lamb meat is better than this old donkey's meat; it is soft and tasty." He said, "Very well. Your meat is of no use anyway; you are old." The donkey said, "Then come. I shall hold up my foot and you pull the shoe off." The donkey lifted his foot, and the wolf leapt to pull off the shoe. At once the donkey struck him in the mouth with a mighty kick. Brother, neither nose nor teeth were left in their place. The wolf ran off screaming with a mouth full of broken teeth. On the road he met a fox, who asked, "What happened to you?" The wolf said, "Before, my trade was butchery: eating sheep and lambs. Today, unfortunately, I became a blacksmith, and blacksmithing has such work in it. That donkey's kick landed hard in my teeth."

title: Two Brothers
text_english:
Two Brothers This is the tale of two brothers. One of them was very clever, and the other was somewhat simple-minded. All the inheritance from their father was one plough, one cow, one blanket, and one fruit tree. One day the clever brother said, "Come, let us make an agreement." The poor brother asked, "What kind of agreement?" He answered, "During the day, when it is long, you may take the blanket; at night I shall take it. Of the cow, the front clean part is yours, and the hind part, which is filthy, is mine. Of the tree, the roots in the ground are yours, and the upper, fruit-bearing part is mine." The poor brother agreed: "Very well; whatever you say is right." Every day the poor brother gave the cow fodder and water, and his brother drank the milk. He watered the tree, and his brother ate the fruit. In the daytime his brother took the blanket. When the poor brother said, "Give me some also," the other said, "The cow's front part is yours and the hind part is mine. The milk is in the hind part, so it is mine; the fruit is on the upper part of the tree; and at night the blanket is mine." The poor brother said nothing, because he was simple. One day a kinsman came to his house and saw that all the work was being done by that simple brother, while all the benefit was being eaten by the other brother. He opened the simple brother's understanding and said, "In the daytime, wet the blanket, and at night give it to your brother." That night, The brother said, "Bring the blanket so I may sleep." The other went and brought the blanket. When the first looked, the blanket was wet. He asked, "Why have you made this wet?" The other answered, "In the daytime it is mine, and with this blanket I can do whatever I want." When his brother heard this, his heart sank and he said to himself, "By God, this one has understood the matter."

Morning came. The brother went to milk the cow. When he sat down to milk it, the foolish brother calmly took a stick and struck the cow on the head. The cow jumped and bucked. His brother became angry and said, "What are you doing? Let me milk her." He answered, "The front part of the cow is my share; I may do whatever I want with it." In short, the brother could not milk the cow.

Then he went to pick fruit. When he had climbed up into the tree, the other brother took an axe and began chopping at the trunk below. His brother said, "What are you doing? You will kill me." He answered, "The lower part of the tree is my share; I may do with it whatever I want." When he said this, his brother understood that everything had turned against him. At last he said, "Very well. Come; we shall divide the fruit and eat it together, sleep under the blanket together at night, and drink the cow's milk together." Evil intention is the calamity that falls upon one's own head.

title: The Div and Digho
text_english:
The Div and Digho Once there was a man named Digho. One night Digho saw a fire on a patch of his land. Beside the fire sat a little black div [demon or giant]. Digho called to the div and said, "Get out of my garden!" The div answered, "No, I shall sit here. I am sitting on top of a treasure." Digho said, "A treasure! If the treasure is inside my garden, then the treasure is mine. Leave my garden, and I shall take the treasure."

The div said, "For two years give me half of whatever you plant. After that the treasure will be yours; otherwise it will not be good for you." Digho said, "Very well. Whatever is above the earth, you take; whatever is under the earth, I shall take." The div was pleased. Digho planted potatoes. When the div came for his share, he saw only yellow, spoiled leaves, while Digho took all the potatoes.

The div became angry and said, "Next year we shall do the opposite. Whatever is under the earth I will take, and whatever grows above the earth you will take." Digho said, "Very well." Then Digho planted wheat. When the wheat ripened, Digho harvested it. The div came and cried, "Am I to take only the straw and roots?" He went away in anger. Digho took the treasure, laughed, and departed.

title: The Lion, the Wolf, and the Fox
text_english:
The Lion, the Wolf, and the Fox There was, or there was not, a lion, a wolf, and a fox. All three of them lived in one forest, and most of the time the wolf and the fox ate from what remained of the lion's hunt. But one day the wolf said to the fox, "What do you and I lack compared with the lion? We too will go hunting with the lion." The fox said, "Good; you and I too will go hunting with the lion." Then both of them went before the lion and said, "We too will go hunting with you." The lion said in his heart, "Although it is not fitting for a lion to wander with such little animals, I will go with them and see what they do." So the lion moved on ahead, and the wolf and the fox followed. While they wandered in the forest, the wolf rejoiced in his heart and said, "Today I shall divide the hunt with the lion and eat well." The lion understood the wolf's intention and said to himself, "Today I shall settle your account."

In short, the lion, the wolf, and the fox went into the forest and hunted a cow, a sheep, and a goat. They brought all three to the place that was the lion's home. Then the lion said to the wolf, "Wolf, divide these." The wolf said, "They are already divided. The cow is yours because you are large; the sheep is mine because I am smaller than you; and the goat is the fox's because he is small." The lion said to the wolf, "Come forward." When the wolf came forward, the lion struck him and tore off his head, saying, "Have you now come to divide with me? Your condition could have been worse than this."

Then the lion said to the fox, "Fox, come and divide these." The fox came forward and said, "Master, this needs no dividing. This goat is for your breakfast, this sheep is for your midday meal, and this cow is for your evening meal." The lion said, "You are very clever. Where did you learn such cleverness?" The fox said, "From the severed head of the wolf."

In this tale the wolf and the fox are not content with the food the lion leaves for them. They go hunting with the lion, and the wolf tries to divide equally with him. The lion understands the wolf's intention and tears off his head. When the fox sees the wolf's severed head, he divides the animals according to the lion's desire. This tale teaches us to be content with whatever God gives, and to govern our desire so that we stay far from trouble and difficulties. As the well-known saying goes, "A large morsel tears the mouth."

title: The Jackal Who Fell into the Dyer's Vat
text_english:
The Jackal Who Fell into the Dyer's Vat Once there was a pack of jackals in a forest. Wherever that pack of jackals went, they went together. One day, while the pack was wandering near a village, one of them got lost, and the others began searching for him. They looked everywhere, but they could not find him. The other jackals grew tired and sat down to rest. While they were resting, the lost jackal arrived. They asked him, "Where had you gone that you became so many-coloured? We searched everywhere, but could not find you." The lost jackal said, "Where I went is not important. Tell me this: what difference is there now between me and a peacock?"

The other jackals laughed and said, "Do not go after such talk. A peacock has its own walk, its own grace, and much beauty. Can you walk like a peacock?" The lost jackal said, "Why should I not be able to? I can walk better than a peacock!" The other jackals said, "Begin, so that we may see." When the dyed jackal began to walk, the other jackals burst into loud laughter and said, "Tell the truth: where did you become coloured like this, that you now appear to yourself to be a peacock?"

Then the lost jackal began his story. "As I was walking along," he said, "I suddenly fell into a dyer's vat and became many-coloured. When I came out of the vat and looked at myself, I saw that I did not differ from a peacock at all." The others laughed again and said, "From your walk it became clear that you are the same old jackal. Remember: a jackal never becomes a peacock merely by changing colour."

In this tale a jackal falls into a dyer's vat and believes that he is no different from a peacock. But when the other jackals test him, they see that he is the same old jackal, only coloured. The story teaches us that if a person does not have a good character, even if he arranges his outward appearance well, his character will still not become good. The well-known saying says, "A nature that comes with milk disappears only with death."

title: The King's Strange Dreams
text_english:
There was, or there was not, in ancient times a king who ruled over a great kingdom. One night the king dreamed that foxes were raining down from the sky. The dream troubled him greatly. However much he thought about it, he could not interpret it. When his own reason failed, he called his ministers and told them the dream so that they might interpret it. But the ministers were bewildered and could find no meaning. At last one minister said, "Your Majesty, the interpretation of your dream is difficult for us, but we know an old man whose work is interpreting dreams. If you summon him, he may interpret your dream." The king accepted the advice and sent for the old man.

When the old man came, the king told him the dream. The old man was confused by what he heard and asked the king for three days' time. The king granted it and promised a large reward. For three days the old man thought, but no clue came to him. He went toward the palace hopeless and sorrowful, and on the way remembered the king's promised reward. Because of greed he made many interpretations in his heart, but none satisfied him. As he went, he saw a snake coiled in the sun. He meant to turn aside, but the snake raised its head and said, "Old man, why are you so hopeless and sad?" The old man sighed and told the snake that the king had dreamed foxes falling from the sky, and that he had not found the interpretation. The snake laughed and asked whether the king had promised a reward. The old man said yes. The snake said, "The interpretation is easy. If you give me half of the reward, I shall tell it to you." The old man said, "Half is little. If you tell me the interpretation, I shall give you all the reward." The snake said, "Tell the king that in your land many flatterers and fox-like people have increased; they deceive the people."

The old man was delighted, hurried to the palace, and gave the interpretation. The king was very pleased and gave him a saddlebag full of gold and jewels. On his way home, the old man remembered his promise to give half the reward to the snake. He put down the saddlebag to divide it, but the gold and jewels became sweet in his heart. He took them all and said to himself, "What use are gold and jewels to a snake? I shall not meet him face to face again."

After some time the king dreamed again, this time that wolves were raining from the sky. Again the ministers could not interpret it, and again the old man was summoned. He asked for three days and went to the snake's house, hoping for help. The snake was coiled outside. Seeing the old man, the snake laughed and asked where he had been and why he was sad again. The old man thought, "What a simple snake," cleared his throat, and said that the king had dreamed wolves raining from the sky. The snake said, "I will interpret it on the condition that this time you truly give me half the king's reward." The old man said, "I agree; this time I will give you all the reward." The snake said, "Tell the king that in your land wolf-like people are increasing. If you do not think of your people, those wolf-like people will tear them apart." The old man told the king, received another large reward, and went home. Then greed entered his heart again. He thought, "If I give all this to the snake, nothing will remain for me. Better to kill the snake and keep the reward." He went to the snake's house with a sword and struck, but the snake escaped into his hole, losing only his tail. The old man thought he had killed him and went home.

After a long time the king sent for the old man again. This time he had dreamed that sheep were raining from the sky. The old man again took three days, but found no interpretation. Thinking the snake was dead, he had no one to help him. When the three days ended, he went hopelessly toward the palace. Passing the snake's house, he saw the snake coiled outside. He was both happy and ashamed. The snake laughed and asked why he was sad. The old man said softly, "I am ashamed before you. I wronged you and regret what I did. I do not know how to ask forgiveness." The snake said, "Recognizing your wrong is itself a good deed, and I forgive you, for greatness lies in forgiveness, not in revenge. Now tell me why you are troubled." The old man said, "The king dreamed that sheep were raining from the sky." The snake said, "Tell the king that the people of his land have become just; they live peacefully and harmlessly, and everyone is content with his right."

The old man rejoiced, gave the interpretation, and the king rewarded him more than before. This time he took the whole reward to the snake and cried, "Snake, come out! I have brought the entire reward for you." The snake came out, looked at the gold and jewels, and said, "I have no need of these. Let them all be yours." The old man wondered, "Why did you ask for half the earlier rewards?" The snake said, "I wanted the dream's interpretation to become clear to me. In truth, you yourself were the interpretation. The first time you were fox-like: you deceived me and did not keep your word. The second time you became like a wild wolf and wounded me. The third time you came like a sheep, peaceful, content with your right, pure of heart, and brought me the whole reward." The old man understood the truth, regretted his deeds, asked the snake's pardon, and went home. As the sayings of Solomon say, "A poor man who is honest is better than a rich man who goes astray," and the proverb says, "A greedy man is never satisfied."

title: Advice Gives Wisdom
text_english:
In the name of God, who gives life, and gives the pen the power to write. Wisdom Given as Advice Will Soon Be Finished There was a foolish man who had a wise wife. Whatever advice his wife gave him, he did the opposite. One day he went to the river to bathe and took off his clothes, and when he entered the water, his clothes were carried away. When he had finished bathing, he saw that his clothes were gone. He wandered about naked and bewildered. Just then he saw people carrying a corpse toward the graveyard. A thought came to him, and he went by the corpse, thinking that if he hid beneath the bier no one would see him. The people said, "This man is a corpse-thief! He is uncovering the dead and taking away its shroud." They beat him soundly. He remained there, aching and bruised, until evening. When night fell he went home, and his wife asked, "Son, why were you so late?" He said, "From this day on you know nothing of me. "Today people beat me and drove me out," the man said. His wife asked, "What had you done?" He told her what had happened. His wife said, "When people see a funeral, they say, 'May God forgive him,' and 'May God give you patience.'" So he learned from his wife to say, "May God forgive him," and "May God give you patience."

One day, as he passed through the village, he saw that there was a wedding gathering. He remembered his wife's words and went to the house where there was celebration, saying, "May God forgive him. May God give you patience." The people said, "This ill-omened man turns our happiness into grief." They gathered, beat him with sticks and kicks, and left his whole body bruised and black. Limping, he reached home. His wife said, "What happened to you today?" Angry at her, he said, "No one is worse off than a man who listens to his wife's words." Then he told what he had done. His wife understood that it had been a wedding and said, "Fool, that was a wedding! At weddings people help and offer congratulations."

The foolish man learned from his wife the words "help" and "congratulations." Another day he went into the fields and saw two boys fighting. In his own mind the madman wanted to help both of them, so he slapped and punched each boy, striking one and then the other. Soon the fathers, mothers, and relatives of both boys heard and came running. They said, "What is happening? Why are you beating both boys?" The man said, "I am helping both of them." They became angry and beat him well with sticks and fists until he was torn and bruised all over. He came home and complained to his wife, "These people do not understand help. I helped their boys and they beat me half dead." His wife said, "Simple man, you struck people's children; of course they would beat you. When two people fight, others step between them, say soothing words, and separate them."

The foolish man learned the phrase "peace, peace" from his wife. Some time later, when he was taking cattle into the mountains, he saw two bulls fighting. He went to separate them, stepped between them, and said, "Peace, peace, greetings, greetings! Do not fight. What has happened that you fight?" But the two bulls struck him and tossed him until their horns met over him. The saying is true: "A bad man does not become good by advice, and an old thing is not made new by patching." It is also true that a wife's wisdom does not belong to a foolish husband.

title: The Miserly Man and the Snake
text_english:
There was, or there was not, in ancient times a miserly man who would stop at nothing in order to become rich. When guests came to his house, he gave them dry bread, and when he himself travelled, before leaving he told his wife to keep household expenses very low.

One day in a nearby place cattle and sheep were for sale. Without delay the miser rode there on his horse to buy some. On the way he saw a tin box, got down from his horse, and opened it to see what was inside. As soon as he lifted the lid, a large snake sprang out, wrapped itself around his neck, and began to choke him. However much the miser cried, no one heard him. He tried to pull the snake away, but could not. He said, "O snake, why have you wrapped yourself around my neck? What harm have I done you?" The snake said, "Have you not heard the proverb, 'For goodness, evil is repaid'?" The miser said, "No, that proverb is not true. In return for goodness there is goodness. I freed you from the box; I did you good, and you should let me go." The snake said, "I do not accept your word; my word is true."

The miser said, "Let us ask a few others. Whatever they say, we must both accept. If your word is proved true, kill me; if mine is true, let me go." The snake agreed. First they asked the miser's sheepdog, "Is it true that evil is the reward for good?" The sheepdog turned to the miser and said, "For many years I have guarded your sheep, and not one has been eaten by wolves, but have you ever given me or your shepherd anything except mouldy bread?" The man turned pale, and the snake said, "You heard the answer. Now I should bite you." Trembling, the miser asked to question the goats and sheep. They said, "Yes, it is true. Year after year we give this man lambs, kids, milk, and wool, but he does not think of us. He leaves us on dry ground where there is neither water nor grass."

The frightened miser asked to question his camels. The old camel sighed and said, "All these young camels you see were born from me and raised for this man, yet he does not think of us. We have no full water or fodder and no good place to stay." The miser's hands and feet shook with fear, and he asked to question a human being. They went to his daughter-in-law. Though she was full of sorrow because of her father-in-law, she could not hide what was in her heart. She said, "Although this man has plenty of wealth, he has never given us good clothing or good food. His demand is always that we work day and night in his house so that his wealth may grow even more."

The miser was astonished by her answer and tried to satisfy the snake in another way. "O snake," he said, "your word is true: evil is repaid for good. It is true that I am miserly, dry-handed, and narrow-hearted. But from now on I shall try to change my nature. Please let me go." The snake said, "I shall not be deceived by your words, and I shall not leave you alive." Then it bit him, and he died. All the property he had scraped together through miserliness remained to his wife, children, and others, while he took nothing with him except a shroud. The well-known saying is: "The miser gathers, and the spenders eat."

title: The First Book of Aesop
text_english:
The wolf and the crane: A greedy wolf was eating an animal he had killed when a small bone stuck in his throat. He could not swallow it, and after a while his throat hurt badly. He wandered everywhere, groaning and seeking someone to remove the bone. He promised anything to whoever would take it out. A crane agreed. The wolf lay on his side and opened his mouth wide. The crane put his head into the wolf's jaws, loosened the bone, and pulled it out. Then he asked for the promised reward. The wolf laughed, showed his teeth, and said, "Be sure that putting your head into a wolf's mouth and bringing it out whole is your reward." Gratitude and greed do not live together.

The man and the snake's young: A countryman accidentally stepped on the tail of a snake, and the snake bit his son, who died. The father seized an axe, chased the snake, and cut off its tail. To avenge itself, the snake bit and killed many of the man's cattle and sheep, causing him great loss. The farmer thought he should make peace. He took bread and honey to the snake's hole and said, "Let us forget hatred and forgive one another. You had the right to punish my son, and I had the right to take revenge." The snake answered, "No. Take your gift away. You can never forget your son's death, and I can never forget my wounded tail. A wound may be forgiven, but it is not forgotten."

The town mouse and the country mouse: A town mouse visited his cousin in the village. The country mouse welcomed him with all his heart and set before him beans, dried meat, cheese, and bread. The town mouse lifted his nose and said, "Cousin, I do not understand how you eat this poor food. Come with me and I will show you how one ought to live." They went to the city and at midnight entered a great dining room where leftovers lay on the table. They ate cakes, pastries, and delicious foods, but suddenly heard barking. The country mouse asked what it was. "Only the house dog," said the town mouse. "Only a dog?" said the country mouse. "I do not like such music at supper." Two big ugly dogs entered, and both mice ran. The country mouse said goodbye, saying, "Beans in peace are better than cakes and pastries in fear."

The crow and the fox: A fox saw a crow flying with a piece of cheese in its beak. The crow sat on a branch. The fox thought, "That cheese must be mine, for I am a fox." He stood beneath the tree and said, "Good day, Lady Crow. How beautiful you look today! How shining are your feathers and bright your eyes. Surely your voice is sweeter than every other bird's. Sing only one verse for me and I shall call you queen of the birds." The crow raised her head and opened her beak to sing; the cheese fell to the ground. The fox snatched it and said, "Good. This is what I wanted. In exchange for the cheese I give you advice for the future: never trust a flatterer."

The sick lion: A lion, sick and near death, came out of his cave for fresh air. The animals he had hunted gathered around. Seeing him dying, they said, "Now the time has come for the lion to answer." The bear came and bit him; the bull gored him; the goat insulted him. Last, the donkey, seeing there was no danger, turned and kicked the lion several times in the face. The lion groaned, "This is death within death. Only cowards insult the noble at the hour of death."

The donkey and the dog: A master came to the stable where his beasts of burden were kept. Among them was a donkey he liked, giving it good water and fodder and using it for riding. His dog came too, danced, jumped about him, and rejoiced. The master took a tasty morsel from his pocket and threw it to the dog, then sat down to direct his workers. The dog sprang into his lap and the master stroked his head. Seeing this, the donkey freed himself from the manger, began to bray and kick, and tried to behave like the dog. He went to sit in the master's lap and put his feet on him. The servants fell upon the donkey with sticks and pitchforks, teaching him that clowning and bad manners are no jest.

The lion and the mouse: A lion was sleeping when a mouse ran over his back. The lion woke, caught the mouse under his paw, and opened his mouth to eat him. The mouse cried, "O king, forgive me this once. I shall never forget your kindness. Who knows? One day I may be of help to you." The lion liked the mouse's words and let him go. Later the lion was caught in a net. Hunters tied him to a tree while they went to fetch something to carry him away. The mouse happened to pass, saw the lion trapped, gnawed through the net, and freed the king of the forest. He said, "Did I not tell you that one day I might be useful? A small friend can become a powerful friend."

The lark and the other birds: A farmer sowed flaxseed in a field where a lark and other birds were feeding. The lark warned the birds to pick up every seed, or they would regret it. They ignored him. The flax grew, was harvested, spun into thread, and woven into a net. The birds who had disregarded the lark's advice were caught in a net made from the flax. The lark said, "Did I not tell you? Dry up the seed of mischief before it grows, or it will destroy you."

The frogs asking for a king: In a pond a crowd of frogs lived happily, splashing in the water without fear. Some said, "This is not right. We need a ruler to make laws and govern us." They asked the mighty emperor for a ruler. He laughed at their noise and threw them a block of wood. It splashed into the pond and frightened them, but when they saw it did not move they climbed on it and danced. Soon they asked again for a real ruler. This angered the emperor, and he sent a stork, who ate them one by one. They regretted their request too late. No government is better than a cruel government.

title: The Second Book of Aesop
text_english:
The Mountain That Fell into Trouble: One day the people of a village heard that a mountain had fallen into difficulty and distress. Smoke rose from the mountain's summit. The earth shook; trees struck one another and fell; pieces of rock slid and broke into fragments. The people understood that a dangerous event was taking place. They gathered in one place and waited and waited, but nothing happened. At last there was a powerful earthquake, and a great crack opened in the waist of the mountain. All the people dropped to the ground on their knees and waited for the earthquake to end. In the end, a tiny little mouse sprang out of the crack, raised its head, and came toward them. When the people saw this scene, they said, "Its clamour was great, but what it produced was small."

The flock of hares and the frogs: The hares were overcome with fear and thought their situation was unbearable, but when they came near a pond a crowd of frogs, frightened by them, jumped into the water. The hares said, "Our condition is not as bad as it seemed; there are others more afraid than we are."

The wolf and the kid: A kid climbed onto a wall and looked around. Suddenly he saw a wolf below. From his safe place he poured insults on his enemy: "Killer, thief, what are you doing here among respectable people? How dared you come where everyone knows your deeds?" The wolf said, "Go on, young friend. When danger is far away, courage and boasting are easy."

The woodcutter and the snake: On a cold winter day a woodcutter was returning slowly from his work when he saw something black on the snow. Coming closer, he found a snake that appeared dead. He pitied it, took it home, warmed it, and put it near the fire. The children watched as the snake slowly came to life. One bent down and touched it, and the snake raised its head to strike. The woodcutter seized his axe and cut the snake in two, saying, "Ah, one must not do good to the wicked."

The bald man and the fly: On a hot summer day a bald man sat on a rock. A fly came buzzing and sat on his head, biting him again and again. The man struck at the fly with his hand and hit his own head hard. The fly troubled him again. This time the bald man used his reason and said, "You injure yourself when you count a low creature as your enemy."

The fox and the stork: A fox and a stork became acquainted and seemed outwardly to be friends. One night the fox invited the stork to dine and, as mockery, set before him soup in a flat dish. The fox could eat easily, but the stork could only wet the tip of his beak. He left the table hungry. The fox said, "I am sorry the food was not to your liking." The stork answered, "No matter. I hope you will be my guest and dine with me." A few days later the fox came to the stork's house. The food was in a long-necked jug with a narrow mouth. The fox could not put his snout inside and could only lick the outside. The stork said, "I am not sorry. It is turn for turn: repay evil with evil."

The fox and the mask: A fox wandered into the storeroom of a theatre and suddenly noticed a glittering face staring at him. He was frightened, but when he looked closely he saw it was only a mask used by actors. The fox said, "Ah, you look like a very fine person, if only you had a brain."

The crow and the peacocks: A crow dared to enter the ground where peacocks walked. He found feathers shed by the peacocks and tied them to his tail, then strutted among them. The peacocks recognized him at once, attacked him with their beaks, and took back their feathers. The crow returned to the other crows, but they had seen his behaviour and were angry with him too. They said, "Good feathers do not make a good bird."

The frog and the bull: A little frog told his father, who stood beside a pool, "I saw a monster as large as a mountain. It had two horns, a long tail, and split hooves." The father said, "My child, that was the farmer's white bull. He is not so large; he is only a little bigger than I am. Watch." The frog puffed himself up and asked, "Was he this big?" The little frog said, "Bigger, father, much bigger." The frog puffed and puffed again until he burst. Pretending to be what you are not destroys you.

The bat, the birds, and the beasts: A great war nearly broke out between the birds and the wild animals. As both armies moved to the field, the bat wondered which side to join. When birds came and asked him to fight with them, he said, "I am an animal." Later, when beasts came and asked him to fight with them, he said, "I am a bird." Fortunately there was no war and both sides made peace. The bat went to the birds to join their celebration, but they rejected him. He went to the beasts, but they too knew his words and drove him away. The bat said to himself, "Now I understand: if you take no one's side, no one becomes your friend."

title: The Third Book of Aesop
text_english:
The stag and the hunter: A stag went to drink at a pool and saw his reflection in the water. He praised his horns: "Where can anyone find such splendid antlers? If only my legs were worthy of this fine crown. What a pity that my legs are thin and weak." Just then a hunter appeared. The stag ran swiftly on those nimble legs and vanished from the hunter's eyes, but he entered trees with low branches, and his horns became caught. The hunter reached him. The stag said, "Alas! We often dislike what is useful to us."

The snake and the file: A snake entered a smith's or weapons shop and crawled among the tools. Suddenly he felt a file scraping his body. He tried to bite it, but his fangs made no mark on iron. In anger he attacked again and again, uselessly. It is foolish to struggle against what cannot be harmed by your blows.

The man and the forest: A man went to the forest carrying an axe head without a handle. He begged the forest to give him a small branch for a necessary task. The trees, being simple-minded, gave him one of their best branches. The man made a handle from it, returned, and began cutting the trees one by one. Only then did they understand that they had acted foolishly and had given their enemy the means to destroy them.

The dog and the wolf: A gaunt wolf, nearly dead from hunger, saw a domestic dog passing. The dog said, "Cousin, I see how you have become. This life has ruined you. Why not find work with me, where you will always have bread?" The wolf agreed. The dog said he would take him to his master and share his work. On the way the wolf noticed a rubbed place on the dog's neck and asked about it. The dog said, "It is nothing; only the mark of the collar and chain they put on me at night. At first it scratches a little, but one grows used to it." The wolf asked, "Only that? Farewell, Master Dog. It is better to die hungry than to live fat as a slave."

The stag in the cattle stable: Hunting dogs chased a stag. He escaped them by entering a cattle stable and hiding under the straw, with only the tips of his antlers showing. Soon the hunters came and searched, but found nothing and left. A little later the owner of the stable came, looked around carefully, and noticed something unusual in the straw. "What are those two strange things above the straw?" he asked. The servants searched and found the stag, and he was killed. People learned that nothing remains hidden from the eye of its owner.

The fox and the grapes: On a hot summer day a fox walked hungrily through a vineyard and saw ripe, fleshy grapes hanging from a vine. "That cluster would end my thirst," he said. He ran and jumped but missed it. Again and again he tried, but failed. At last he gave up the desire to eat them, walked away with his nose in the air, and said, "It is clear the grapes are sour." It is easy to count a thing worthless when you cannot obtain it.

The horse, the hunter, and the stag: A quarrel arose between a horse and a stag. The horse went to a hunter and asked for help in taking revenge. The hunter agreed, but said, "If you want victory over the stag, allow me to put iron in your mouth and a saddle on your back. I shall guide you with the bridle and ride you to bring down your enemy." The horse accepted. With the hunter's help he defeated the stag. Then he said, "Now remove these things from my mouth and back." The hunter replied, "Not so fast, friend. I could free you from bridle and stirrup, but it suits me for you to remain as you are."

The peacock and Juno: A peacock asked Juno, "High lady, I wish that the nightingale's voice would be added to my beauty and splendour." Juno refused. The peacock insisted that he was her favourite bird. Juno said, "Be content. You have many other gifts. No one can be first in everything."

The lion and the fox: The first time a fox saw a lion, he was so frightened that he ran and hid in the forest. The second time he saw the lion, he stood at a safe distance and let him pass. The third time, he came near, greeted the lion, asked after his household, and spoke as if they were old friends. Then he turned his tail and went away without showing respect. Too much familiarity diminishes reverence.

title: The Hunter and the Bird
text_english: One day, he caught a bird in his trap. The bird appeared and said: Hey sir! You have eaten many meats throughout your life and you have never turned; Don't die even by eating this small body of mine. If I release you, I will give you three words of advice, so that prosperity and good luck will come to you. I will tell you the first thing when I released you, the second thing I will tell you when I sit on the roof of your house and the third thing I will tell you when I sit on the tree. Seemingly agreeing, the bird said: You will never believe in impossible words. It seems that he released him without any delay, he sat on the roof of the bird and said: The second thing of Pand: Never go after the past and don't worry about what you have lost before, because it is of no use. The bird sat on a branch of a tree and said: O sir! There is a bird in my belly, which weighs ten dirhams, but unfortunately, the fate of you and your children was not in it, otherwise you would have become very rich with it. It seems that he was very sad to hear this, so he got up and said, "What did I do?" The bird said to him with a smile: I advised you a few moments ago not to follow the past, either you did not understand my advice or you are deaf? The bird said: My second advice is not to believe those words that are far from possible. Oh simple! My total weight is not more than three (3) dirhams. How is it possible that a chicken weighing ten dirhams is in my stomach? It seems that he was lost in the sea of thoughts for a few moments, then he said: "O clever bird, you are very precious, tell me the third thing of Pind. " Speaking advice to ignorant and sleepy people is like sowing seeds on rocky ground.

title: The Bremen Musicians
text_english: Once upon a time, a farmer in Germany had a donkey. The donkey had worked well for many years, but with the passage of time, the donkey had become old and weak, it could not work as well as before, so one day the farmer decided to sell the donkey. When the hare understood this, he was very sleepy. He did not expect such a result in return for his good work, so he decided to run away and find another job. He said to himself: I will go to Burman and I will be a musician there! So the donkey was walking on the road towards Burman. He saw a dog sitting on the road. The donkey said: - Hello dog! what are you doing? The dog said: - I am trying to find another house for myself. My husband kicked me out because I'm old and can't hunt. The donkey said: - Come with me. I am going to Burman to study music. The dog immediately stood up and walked with the donkey. After a while they saw a cat sitting on the side of the road. The donkey said: Hello cat! what are you doing? Peshi said: - I am trying to find a new house for myself. My husband kicked me out because I'm stubborn and can't catch mice. The dog said: - Come with us. We go to Burman, where the musicians are. The cat immediately stood up and walked with them. After a while, he saw a chicken that was singing the adhan very loudly. The donkey said to him: - Hello, hen. But do you call the adhan so forcefully? The chicken said: - I have very little time to live because my husband said that the guests are coming tomorrow and they will kill me. As I like to call the call to prayer, I call call to prayer in this short time. With that he called another adhan. The cat said to him: - Come with us. We go to Burman, where the musicians are. The chicken immediately sat on the donkey's back and walked with them. When it was evening, they reached a forest and fell under a tree that was lying. A chicken called the call to prayer and said: - I see a house there. Let's go there. It is possible that those people will give us food and water. Donkey, cat, dog and chicken all went to that house. The dog said: - This is a good place, but how do we enter the house? Let's play music for him. The donkey said: - It's a good thing. Maybe they like to let us in and give us some food and drink. So the donkey put its two front legs on the top of the kilkin, the dog sat on the donkey's back, the cat sat on the dog's head and the chicken sat on the cat's head and recited the ghazal to all of them. The donkey brayed loudly, the dog brayed loudly, the cat chirped loudly, and the chicken crowed loudly. They shouted slogans so loudly that they were defeated. That person, who was actually a thief, got very angry and ran away from the door. The animals were a little surprised that the people had run away, but they thought that they had gone to tell other people how they had heard good music. The animals entered the house through Mati Handari, sat around the table and started eating. In a very short time, all the food on the table was opened. When she died, she put out the fire and everyone slept in one place. The cat was on the side of the fireplace, the dog was in front of the door, the hare was on the grass in the inn, and the chicken was sleeping on top of the fireplace where the parrot's tail was hanging high. The thief was hiding in the forest and was looking at him. When he saw that the fire had died down, he sent someone to see who was in their house. When that person reached home, Mati Handari entered the house. It was dark, nothing could be seen and no sound could be heard. There were only two groups in Nagari. The thieves thought that they were dirty. But he was wrong. They were basically cat eyes. The robbers tried to kill him, but the cat brought him back. The thief ran away, so he ran to the door, but the dog at the door caught the thief's leg. The thief shouted and rushed to the inn, but the donkey was waiting there and he gave the thief such a strong word that he flew into the air and fell back to the bloody place from the side of Mati Handari. In all this noise, the chicken woke up and loudly called adhan in the ear of the thief. The thief left the house, went back to his friends, crying and said: - A witch lives in our house! Look how he made my nose! At the door, he stopped a worker with a knife. Look at how he made my leg shine. There is another big worker in his inn whose legs are like donkeys. See how I beat him. But the worst is the one who sits on the floor and shouts! When the thieves heard this, they realized that they could never go back to their home, so they went to another forest. The donkey and his friends liked the house of thieves, so they stayed and played music like real musicians, even if they never reached Burman. From this nickel we learn that if someone is old, we should not forget to serve him and help him when he is weak and not look down on him. (From Germany)

title: The Two Japanese Frogs
text_english: Once upon a time there lived two frogs in Japan. The house of an old man was a dump in Osaka (which is a poor city in Japan). Billy Changzhi lived in a river in Tokyo (which is the capital of Japan and is a very crooked city). One day the king of Osaka asked to see Tokyo and the king of Tokyo asked him to go to Osaka once. They both left their house at the same time. There was a big hill between these two cities. The two birds reached the hill at the same time. When they saw each other, they greeted each other, talked to each other and told each other where they wanted to go. A sparrow said to the cat: - I wish we were a little bigger like other animals. Then we will be able to see the other city and know how it is and decide whether to go there or not. She said: - This is not a big problem. Let us strengthen ourselves and stand on our back legs, then we will be able to see each other's cities. With that he did it. But they forgot that the eyes of all the frogs are on their heads. So when they did that, they actually went back to the cities they came from. The frog of Osaka said: - This is strange! Tokyo is like Osaka! The city of Tokyo said: - Osaka is like Tokyo again! So they turned back to their homes from the road and until the end of their lives, they were satisfied that Tokyo and Osaka were the same, that they were basically the opposite of the absolute. From this nickel we learn that we should not judge by sight alone. Maybe what we have seen is not the truth. (From Japan)

title: The Bear and the Locust
text_english: One day a hare was walking on the road, he didn't look at the road, he didn't know that he was on the grasshopper's house. The locust was in pain and shouted: - You stop, rabbit! I will be with you. The rabbit laughed and said: - What are you talking about? Does this mean you want to fight me? The locust said: - But no! You gather your people and I will fight tomorrow near the forest! The hare said: - It is right. So tomorrow they both went to the forest. The hares were 15 shrews, 10 foxes, 5 easy and 2 big dogs. There were 100 grasshoppers, 100 locusts, 100 locusts, 100 poisonous insects and 100 scorpions. But the hare could not see the friend of the locust. He said: - Where are your people? As if they ran away! Molkh replied: - No. These are With this, he said to his men: - Come on, friends! Immediately, all the people of the locusts came out of their hiding places and attacked Khars and his men. The grasshopper shouted: - He is fighting. Fighting! They are bigger than us but we are more than them. He said the truth. The hare was the worst injured because the bullies wanted to kill him. When he couldn't take it anymore, he shouted: - Run away! Enter the water! The hare and his people all fell into the river. The hare was about to drown. After that, the hare looks at the ground as it walks. We learn from this nickel not to look down on those who are younger than us. (from a French source)

title: How Stories Came into Being
text_english: Once upon a time, a king called all the animals to him and said: - Who among you can turn a grain of wheat into an ox? All the animals thought that it was impossible, but Sui said: - I will try. So he took a grain of wheat from the king, went to a village and put that grain on the ground. At that time, a hen came and ate the grain. Sui caught that hen and said to her husband: - Look at you! Your hen ate my grain of wheat. The owner of the hen told him: - He does not care. I will give you another grain of wheat. Sui said: - But that grain was given to me by the king. You should give me that chicken. So the owner of the hen was forced to give the hen to the cow. Sui went to another village with the hen. There he asked someone to give them a place for the night. A man gave them a place to spend the night and Sui said to him: - Do not put my hen together with your chickens because it is a very big hen. Keep it with your goats. When she got up in the morning, she went to get her hen, but a goat climbed on the hen and killed it. Soi picked up his dead chicken and said to the owner of the house: - Look at you! Your goat has killed my hen! The owner of the house said: - Forgive me. I will give you another chicken. Sui said: - But that hen was given to me by the king, so she is worth a goat to me. You should give me a goat instead. So the owner of the house was forced to give Sui a goat. Sui went to another village with the goat. There, he asked someone else to give them a place to spend the night. Someone else was born in the village and gave them a place. Sui said to him: - Do not put my goat together with your goats. He is a very warlike goat that does not bite your goats. Put it with your cows. The owner of the house did the same. Tomorrow morning, when she gets up to see her goat, she sees that the goat is dead. A cow was beaten with words. Soi shouted: - Look at you! Your cow has killed my goat! The owner of the house said: - I will give you another goat. Sui said: - But that goat was given to me by the king. She was very important to me. You should give me a cow instead. And he also gave a cow, so he became the owner of a cow and did not pay any money. She stood up to show it to the king. The king said: - Well done! You deserve a reward! Say, what do you want? Sui said: - I want the matrabana that is beside your feet. It was such a jar that when the king wanted to give a nickel to the animals, he would open the jar and a nickel would come out of it. The king said: - I will give it to you, but if you lose it, then you will lose all the nickels forever. He took the bag and went home. He had not gone far when he fell down and fell down. All the nickels came out. Since then, nickels have been around and are in every country in the world. From this nickel, we learn that man can make the impossible possible by means of will, decision and intellect. (from Africa)

title: The Spider and the Bananas
text_english: Once upon a time there was a girl who wanted to be the smartest of all animals. For this reason, he left the world. She took a big bag with her and gave him every smart thing she could find. Wherever she went, her fiancee also carried her, and when she returned home, she held her fiancee on her shoulders. The bridegroom was so heavy that he could not lift the bells without his head. On the road, she saw a trunk. The boy stopped for a while at the pond to drink water and saw that he had eyes in the water. Ghan said happily: - I have to eat some bananas because I am very hungry! But when he went to the water to get the bananas, the bananas were not in the water. He came back and said: - I will drink some water. If he sees that he saw it again! He went to the water again to find bananas, but he did not find them either. The voice came back, but he lowered his head and saw it again. He then went into the water to get bananas, but again he did not find any bananas. Several bezogans who were sitting on a high tree, looked at the bells and said: - What are you doing bells? Ghan said to him: - I am trying to get the banana that I see in the water. Bezogano laughed and said: - Look high, then you will grow your bananas. But the bells could not raise their heads because of the betrothed. She took out the mange, and when she looked hungry, she saw that the banana was hanging from a branch. Ghan saw the image of the banana in the water! The girl was in pain and shouted: - I have a fiance full of wisdom, but what has he benefited me? Bizogani are smarter than me! With that, he hit the fiance with a stone and broke it. The lesson of this nickel is that wisdom cannot be found, bought or stolen. Everyone should have it in their head and train it. (from the country of Iran)

title: The Mosquito and the Lizard
text_english: Once upon a time there was a Khazdika and a cowherd, but both were very poor. One day Khazdaki said to Ghomashi: - Let's go to the forest, we will collect skulls. We will make coconut oil from it and sell it. They went to the forest. Ghomashi said to Khazdaki: - You are dead, drop the skull, I will put it under. But Khazdaki said: - Or, you kill and throw out the skull. Ghumasha brought out the skulls under the tree, then came down to me. But when they reached the house, Khazdaki said: - Take the oil out of the skull, I will take it to the market and sell it.
